Our novel object representation, Neural Descriptor Fields, overcomes the
difficulty of employing graph neural networks for 3D object processing by sidestepping
the need to construct explicit graph structures. In a conventional setting, we employ a
simple fully connected neural network to generate object descriptors. When working among
3D objects, we introduce a novel, 3D equivariant operation called Spherical Swin Transformer
block, designed to maintain 3D object symmetry during processing. By merging these
descriptors and employing a fully connected neural network for object classification, our model
achieves 3D object equivariance without relying on extraneous features or inter-objects
communication. In a multi-object setting, we introduce a novel Neural Descriptor Field, a
directed graph where nodes represent objects and corresponding descriptors, and edges
represent 3D spatial relationships among them. We employ a novel 3D equivariant messagepassing
algorithm among objects, attaining a 3D object representation that retains its intrinsic
properties even after objects are rearranged. In a self-supervised 3D object reconstruction
task, our model excels, outperforming state-of-the-art models that employ graph neural
networks. Moreover, we introduce a 3D object segmentation dataset, called ModelNet-Object, and
multiple 3D object classification datasets, demonstrating the efficacy of our model with
minimal overfitting. Our novel model, along with related code and models, is publicly

consistently superior to competing models, as evident from the results presented in

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining projection clustering and correspondence learning between 2D-3D projections. Projection clustering is used to generate a code that represents optimal projection combinations, codified as GMM parameters. These codes are fed into a decoder that produces a distribution of correspondence constraints. The proposed network architecture, named DeepHMap++, achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art models, as demonstrated by enhanced results on Benchmark Full DOF Pose Estimation and the STL dataset. Code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyangyin/DeepHMap++.

A high-speed camera was used to capture spheres entering water from different distances, both far and close to the water surface. Our analysis focuses on a specific speed range, between 2.3 and 7.8 meters per second, where previous research showed conflicting results regarding the formation of droplets and entrapment of air. High-resolution images from the camera measurements enabled us to accurately determine when and how air becomes trapped and how it influences the shape of the impact zone. Our findings support a previous theory that air becomes trapped when the sphere enters the water at a certain angle of incidence, and we discovered a relationship between this angle and the speed of entry. Over time, the air pocket eventually collapses, and our research explores when and how this happens. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new technique incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Notably, our technique differs from existing methods that can model polymers, such as molecular sequence optimization and fragment linking, offering a distinct way of representing chemical compounds. This new approach is capable of generating predictive models to estimate the physical properties of both monomeric units and the overall polymer, also offering a numerical representation of the polymer's chemical structure that can be used for further analysis or design. Code for this technique is provided in the appendix along with an example of using it to create a model predicting the boiling point of alkanes. This model was subsequently used to identify a previously unknown class of non-symmetrical branched alkanes with specific property ranges. This represents the first application of this technique in identifying a distinct class of chemical compounds. This framework has been named Polymers Inference Framework or PI2. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for a manual analysis by doctors, which can lead to longer diagnosis times. Furthermore, improving this capability takes a considerable amount of time, in part due to lacking standardized data sets for training and testing, which are essential for modeling techniques like artificial neural networks. In response to these challenges, an automatic method was developed called the Dilated Dense Focus Unet (DDAUnet) that incorporates two novel components: a dilated convolution block and a dense focus block. This model excels at accurately identifying and outlining tumors in a single-layer architecture, and its compact design allows it to adapt to limited data scenarios, making it an ideal choice for esophageal tumor segmentation using CT scans. Experimental results showed that the DDAUnet model outperformed existing models in accuracy and low-overhead recall, and it achieved a notable improvement with limited data sets, primarily composed of intestinal organ tumors. Code-mixed languages, which combine two or more languages within a single text, are a common method multilingual speakers use to navigate the challenges of having limited access to information labeled in their native tongue. This code-mingling is observable on social media platforms but less so on formally published documents. As a result, developing effective NLP models that can process multiple languages simultaneously has a significant obstacle to succeeding. This problem is a major hindrance especially for tasks that depend on a large amount of labeled data. This problem affects numerous NLP applications but is particularly challenging for those involving multiple languages, such as machine translation, sentiment analysis, and information retrieval. This issue affects a substantial number of people who speak multiple languages, including users with who know both Hindi and Marathi, with an estimated 80 million native speakers worldwide. This group has a particularly difficult time as both languages have many similarities which code-mingling can take advantage of, yet research on code-mixed NLP typically treats the two languages as if they were independent rather than taking into account their shared features. This problem also presents a major barrier for various applications that can benefit from multilingual abilities, including but not limited to remote information access. This problem is not just an NLP challenge but also a societal one that affects the ability of certain groups to access vital information. This issue demands a more nuanced and complex approach that can handle the intricacies of code-mingling and the diversity of the languages involved. This approach should also allow for sufficient flexibility to accommodate the many variations of code-mingling. This issue and its complexities are illustrated through an analysis of code-mingling in Hindi-English but its principles and challenges are applicable to any pair of languages that have a significant amount of overlap. This research paper encourages other researchers to explore and analyze similar challenges in other language pairs. This issue and its challenges are not just limited to Hindi-English but are a broader, more fundamental problem that affects code-mixed NLP for any pair of languages. This problem and its complexities are not just an NLP challenge but a societal one with the potential to impact a substantial number of people who speak multiple languages. This research paper outlines a plan for a workshop that will delve deeper into the problems, challenges, and diverse variations of code-mingling and explore and analyze similar challenges in other language pairs. This workshop will also provide a platform for sharing data and models that can benefit the research community as a whole. Generating accurate and diverse automatic image descriptions is a complex task that requires extensive knowledge about objects, their relationships and attributes, as well as common language patterns. This challenge is compounded by the limited size of training datasets, which often fall short of capturing these nuances. Proponents of this approach suggest that generating descriptions is similar to translating text, and cite the success of large neural translation models as evidence. While these models have achieved high-quality results in various tasks, they have also been known to produce generic responses. A key issue with using automatic description generators is their tendency to produce diverse, yet often inaccurate and unrelated descriptions. This problem is exacerbated by the lack of constraints used in current generation approaches. To address this limitation, we propose using human-annotated image description datasets as constraints to evaluate automatic generators. Our results show that automatic generators produce a narrow range of descriptions that prioritize certain elements over others, and demonstrate a method for using these datasets to guide generation via reinforcement learning. Tantalum oxide compounds, specifically Ta$_{0.5}$Ta$_{0.5}$O$_5$, exhibit intriguing properties tied to superconductivity and geometric frustration. However, this material lacks a well-defined lattice structure, which makes it particularly hard to research using conventional methods. To overcome this challenge, researchers are using first-principles simulations and Monte Carlo methods for lattice distortions. By examining various configurations using $k$-space and $q$-space scans of energy and magnetic ordering, scientists have successfully identified the most stable and lowest-energy state of Ta$_{0.5}$Ta$_{0.5}$O$_5$. The results show that this material has an intricate, all-in-all-out (AIAO) type of magnetic ordering at room temperature and a $\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}$ lattice structure with a 30-degree rotation. Notably, this research has demonstrated that AIAO type of ordering is extremely rare and requires both geometric frustration and specific lattice configurations to manifest, which may have implications for other materials exhibiting similar conditions. Lastly, the findings suggest that AIAO phase can be converted to the all-in-all-out (AIAO$\rightarrow$AIO) phase through applied pressure, which may offer a valuable strategy for controlling its electronic and magnetic properties. The simulated material has a direct bandgap and the introduction of oxygen vacancies can convert it from a semiconducting to a superconducting state, which may have analogies with other materials, such as TaNCl and TaON. The code used for this research is included in the supplementary materials. The Monte Carlo simulations were validated through comparison with experimental data for another TaO compound, Ta$_{0.5}$Ta$_{0.5}$O$_3$, which exhibits $120^\circ$ bond-orientational order and a $\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}$ lattice structure, and also includes results for another material, Ta$_{0.5}$Ta$_{0.5}$O$_3$ with $60^\circ$ BTO, which may have a AIAO type of ordering. The simulations were performed using the Fleur code and the JARFS supercomputer. This research investigates how the significant population movement known as the Big Shift, which saw people relocate from coastal areas to inland regions, may have influenced the spread of misinformation among Reddit users in the United States. To achieve this, we examined user contributions across different geographic locations before and after the Big Shift, which is hypothesized to have occurred between 2000 and 2010 based on changing census data. Our analysis utilizes a Reddit dataset spanning from June 2007 to June 2019 and incorporates a variety of misinformation indicators, including fact-checking website verifications of false information on Reddit posts. By combining social network analysis and geographic data, our study mapped Reddit user affiliations to inland and coastal regions and tracked changes over time. Our key finding indicates that the Big Shift was associated with increased circulation of misinformation in inland areas, suggesting that changes in population distribution may contribute to the wider dissemination of false information in certain societal contexts. This research offers an initial exploration of a neglected aspect in the study of misinformation and highlights the potential of Reddit data in conjunction with demographic analysis tools in identifying and analyzing factors contributing to the spread of misinformation. Existing theories on social diffusion and network dynamics can be applied to our findings, and future work may build on this research by considering the role of online and offline social networks in the Big Shift and its effects on the distribution of misinformation. Ultimately, this study may have implications for the development of targeted misinformation prevention strategies. For the purpose of this research, the Big Shift refers to population movements reflected in United States census data, specifically the decline of urban coastal populations and the growth of inland populations, as well as analogous geographic shifts evident in Reddit user contributions. Humans employ diverse speech elements during task demonstrations to robots, which are typically learned through audio-only instruction. While both verbal and non-verbal audio cues are used, research has mainly focused on the linguistic aspects, neglecting the significance of intonation, a crucial element in human communication. This study examines how human instructors utilize intonation when demonstrating manipulation tasks and investigates whether a deep learning-based approach can effectively capture these patterns to enhance robotic learning through demonstration. A convolutional neural network was successfully applied to extract relevant features from speech spectra and temporal representations, which were then combined to create a robust set of features to differentiate between similar demonstrations. These findings can be leveraged to develop more efficient robotic learning through demonstration using audio instruction. A simple reinforcement learning system was also constructed to demonstrate the practical utility of this feature extraction method. This research was presented at the 2020 IEEE/RSJ Joint Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems.

A complex field theory is interpreted to operate within a diverse, intricate mathematical framework composed of diverse geometric elements, particularly those identified within the scope of symplectic and Riemannian geometry. Despite the richness of this framework, it maintains remarkable flexibility, allowing it to accommodate a broad category of analytical functions known as Bell functions, which are derived from a fundamental equation known as the Euler-Arnold equation, often with variations such as the Hamilton-Legendre equation and the Euler-Arnold transport equation. Both the basic Euler-Arnold equation and its various iterations possess certain distinctive features that can be used to identify conformal field transformations displaying both scalar and vector characteristics. It is also demonstrated that the complex field theory encompasses multiple conformal transformations, which can be recognized by rearranging the Euler-Arnold equation into an Abelian closure system that is both consistent and explicit. This analytical framework is then applied to derive a comprehensive and explicit expression for the two-loop Casimir effect, which involves a scalar field interacting with itself within a circular cavity formed from a one-plus-three spacetime. This analysis delves into the core of this problem, known as the conformal field theory intricacy, which previous studies had only addressed in a superficial manner. It does so by breaking down the two-loop conformal field integrals into their individual components, which can be analyzed and combined using a closure system generated from the Euler-Arnold equation, with a key contribution being the identification of a novel nontrivial Bell function that was not previously known. This research demonstrates that the Euler-Arnold equation and its associated geometric elements provide the most suitable and flexible framework for predicting the complex and analytical components of the two-loop Casimir effect, which was achieved by demonstrating a way to overcome an analysis obstacle that had been previously reported by other researchers. Conversational agents like robots and voice assistants are becoming ubiquitous in our daily lives and their application domains are continually expanding. Although these systems have achieved a high degree of success, their widespread adoption is hindered by their limited reliability. In fact, it's not uncommon for these agents to provide substandard or even incorrect responses to users. To ensure the quality and dependability of these systems and their widespread adoption, a structured testing approach is desperately needed. Unfortunately, developing well-structured tests for conversational agents in particular, and more generally for interactive systems, proves to be a challenging task. In this paper, we present a comprehensive, user-friendly, and automated testing framework designed to streamline the testing process for conversational agents. This sophisticated system offers an intuitive interface where testers can create and manage tests by inputting desired responses from the agent, as well as specifying the interaction protocols. Furthermore, it includes an assessment tool to measure the effectiveness of these tests and provides detailed feedback on system-performance metrics. We have successfully applied this testing framework to create and execute tests for a real-world conversational agent, and our findings are presented in the paper. Our testing framework is an open-source platform available for public use, and it offers a valuable resource for industry professionals and the academic community alike. All interested parties are invited to contribute to the development of this framework and enhance its capabilities further. This paper and its associated code can be found at www.conversationaltesting.org. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the growing number of users with varied multitype preferences. Existing studies mainly concentrate on intra-domain personalization and homography-based methods with limitations. In this paper, a novel multi-sparse-domain cooperative recommendation framework called MSDCR is proposed, assuming that multiple items from different domains typically prefer different user attributes. Enhancements are made to a comprehensive aspect preference learning model, incorporating sparsity constraints in both user and item domains to capture users' diverse attribute preferences. The framework consists of three key components: (1) a dense connection network for transferring knowledge between domains, (2) a weighted inter-domain fusion module with sparsity constraints to address diverse attribute preferences, and (3) prediction modules for each domain. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of MSDCR, showing it outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines and recommended density-aware and attribute-oriented variants. Moreover, MSDCR's versatility in handling both single-item and multi-item recommendations from multiple domains is showcased, along with an exploration of different sparsity-induced subgraphs from a visualization perspective. The proposed framework and evaluation results are available online for further scrutiny. The code has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyangzeng/MSDCR. The recommended datasets are available at https://github.com/zhengyangzeng/MSDCR/blob/main/datasets. The recommended visualization results are available at https://github.com/zhengyangzeng/MSDCR/blob/main/visualizations. The proposed framework has the potential to handle a wide range of complex, real-world problems involving diverse attribute preferences in multiple sparse domains. In particular, it can be applied to multi-item cross-domain recommendations where multiple items from different domains typically prefer different user attributes, as well as various single-item recommendation scenarios, such as fashion, movie, and music recommendations. The proposed framework can also be used by researchers as a baseline for further enhancements and modifications, such as integrating it with external knowledge, using graph convolutional networks, or exploring different sparsity-induced subgraphs. The Hypatia solver is a new conjugate gradient-based method for solving natural conic equations, extending the capabilities of interior-point methods to exotic convex cones. Building on the Hypatia solver, a new optimization framework called Hypatia.jl is introduced, capable of solving convex optimization problems with a wide array of convex cones. Hypatia.jl also features an interactive Python version of the solver known as Hypatia Py. With Hypatia Py, users can input their own convex optimization problems and visualize the solution spaces of their conic equations. A distinctive aspect of Hypatia Py is its focus on the geometric analysis of convex cones and the visualization of solution spaces. The Hypatia Py application is available online at https://cognitibs.github.io/HypatiaPy/. The Hypatia.jl Julia framework and Hypatia Py Python application are designed to facilitate teaching, research, and development in convex optimization and interior-point methods. They provide users with visual tools for defining, solving, and visualizing natural conic equations and convex optimization problems. The Julia and Python versions of Hypatia share the same underlying solver and cone definitions, enabling the seamless translation of problems between the two environments. The Hypatia.jl framework and Hypatia Py Python application are available on GitHub at https://github.com/CognitiBS/Hypatia.jl and https://github.com/CognitiBS/Hypatia Py, respectively. With over 100 distinct convex cones supported, the Hypatia solver and Hypatia Py application cater to a broad spectrum of applications, from finance and energy to machine learning and statistics. The escalating utilization of magnetic resonance imaging in neuroscience research and clinical applications is prompting hospitals to acquire multiple scanners, making it necessary to create versatile MRI quality control systems that can be shared across sites. Since training such a system on data from each new scanner would be impractical due to the extensive amount of imaging equipment involved, there's a growing interest in developing models that can generalize well across different scanners. In this work, we investigate the hypothesis that effective MRI quality control models can be trained on a single batch of data and effectively generalize across a substantial number of unseen scanners, by exploring the impact of various factors such as image modality, scan parameters, and specific scanners on MRI analysis tasks. To demonstrate the applicability of our findings, we trained and evaluated a series of models on abnormality detection tasks using data from 13 scanners. Our results show that (1) image modality and scan parameters significantly influence the generalization of MRI quality control models and that (2) trained models perform substantially better on scanners with similar acquisition parameters and modality used during training. Furthermore, we introduce a simple yet effective strategy to promote robustness on specific scanners. Our research underscores the importance of considering image modality and scan parameters in MRI quality control development and offers practical guidelines for efficient model training on limited data. With the rapid advancement in MRI technology, models trained on earlier scanners may need to be fine-tuned for newer scanners. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the stability of distribution networks during outages, we developed a decision-making model for individuals that considers the connection between charging their vehicles and restoring or maintaining the power grid in their local area. This model was part of a larger multi-agent optimization framework, also incorporating decision-making models for utility companies and private EV owners, with the goal of minimizing overall costs and ensuring a reliable and stable grid. We validated our model by applying it to a real-world test case in California. The results showed that, in response to a network outage, it's generally more economical for individuals to prioritize charging their vehicles over contributing to grid restoration through load reduction, which could have implications for the effectiveness of this strategy in real-world scenarios. The study and model can be used by utility companies to effectively manage the complex relationship between private EV ownership and distribution network resilience with load management tools. The multi-agent optimization model presented can be adapted for use in other applications, such as microgrid management and transportation planning. The study highlights the need for new economic incentives to encourage private EV owners to contribute to the restoration of the grid in their local area in the event of an outage, which could help reduce the financial burdens and social impacts of such events. The study and model ignore external benefits of this kind of grid resilience services provided by private EV owners, which could take many forms, from reducing the risk of public safety hazards from abandoned vehicles to supporting emergency services and the local economy. The study assumes that the geography of power distribution is the same as the geography of EV charging, which may not always be the case, presenting a potential area for further research. The model developed can be used to identify areas with overlapping distribution grids and EV charging grids that could provide the same level of service, allowing for more efficient and cost-effective grid management, with implications for transportation and energy policy and planning. In our research, we took up the challenge of conducting a large-scale meeting where multiple agents collaborate to reach a common goal. We took a novel approach by dividing the meeting into three distinct phases: an initial dialogue phase where participants introduce themselves, a main phase where the discussion unfolds, and a concluding phase where the meeting reaches its climax. To achieve this, we employed a drive-based motivation model for each agent, combining modules that determine their motivation levels and decision-making policies. We tested this model in a realistic scenario with a large number of agents in a conference setting, using the DialogBRT platform for assistance. Our results showed that the model effectively produces authentic phase transitions and that the drive-based motivation model is highly expressive, able to capture complex patterns even in a small amount of training data. We also explored a variant of the model and found it to be highly competitive, surpassing the performance of DialogBRT in various evaluation metrics. Notably, we demonstrated that the model can produce diverse outcomes even when faced with a large number of identical agents, each with their own distinct personality. Our code is available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/ghr96/MARM. Additionally, we created a large-scale meeting dataset called MAISM, consisting of over 6,000 generated meetings with 5 agents each, available for download on GitHub. We also explored a variant of the model and found it to be highly competitive, surpassing the performance of DialogBRT in various evaluation metrics. We believe this research has significant implications for creating more sophisticated meeting scenarios and for developing a more advanced drive-based motivation model with wide-ranging applications. We studied the fundamental properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds, analyzing their energy spectra, charge distributions, and magnetic moments. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on these materials. Notably, CmSn3 was found to possess a half-filled 4f orbital, while GdSn3 and CmSn3 exhibit anti-ferromagnetic ordering, in contrast to the ferromagnetic behavior found in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series. Our predictions also suggest that the Curie temperature of the GdxCm1-xSn3 series could be quite high, and that these materials have promising magnetocaloric effects and electrical transport properties. Given their unique properties, these compounds have potential for technical and fundamental research applications. Our calculated results are in line with available experimental and theoretical data on these materials. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to ongoing studies of these compounds and provide a foundation for future investigations. Given the limited scope of this work, we suggest some potential areas for future research. In our previous work, we established a formalism for predicting missing particles, which are likely to have been observed in deep inelastic scattering experiments but were not accounted for due to insufficient detector technology at the time. We updated the analysis to incorporate a more precise model of hadron production and expanded the search for several additional particles, including some that may have been identified but were not recorded in the experiments. We also explored potential for new particles to have been created in heavy-ion collisions but were too large to be detected by current experiments. In this paper, we outline the methods used and present numerical results for a broader range of particles, taking into consideration their possible electric charge. We found that many additional baryons and mesons, weighing between 3 and 11 GeV, could have been observed in deep inelastic scattering experiments but were likely missed due to the limited range of charged particles that could be detected at the time. We estimate the cross-sectional area for some of these particles to be in the order of 10 to the power of negative 2, which is comparable to the cross-sectional area of well-known hadrons from the same particle families. We encourage researchers to re-examine their deep inelastic scattering data and heavy-ion collision data for possible evidence of these missing particles. With the advent of next-generation experiments that can detect a wider range of charged particles, we predict a vast array of new baryons and mesons waiting to be discovered in heavy-ion collisions. A one-GeV range of missing particles is predicted to be accessible to the future Electron-Ion Collider, which is capable of precisely measuring the properties of these particles once they are discovered. We propose a list of search criteria for these experiments based on our analysis of deep in elastic scattering data. We also outline the potential for the discovery of new, heavy hadrons that could lie outside the reach of the Electron-Ion Collider, requiring the development of even more advanced experiments with longer detection ranges. With the growing importance of hadron physics in the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model, we emphasize the critical role that experimental discoveries of new hadrons will play in guiding and directing future research in the field. We propose a set of principles for designing future experiments that prioritize the detection of a wide range of charged particles, which will greatly increase the likelihood of discovering new hadrons and opening up a broader range of missing energy for investigation. The Coxeter groups in the B2 foundation have a well-known theorem associating root systems with lattices of subgroups of the Weyl group W, where a non-trivial reflection in W is linked to a specific angle if it isn't 180 degrees, generating 13 distinct lattices. A generalization of this phenomenon to the Bn foundation for n greater than 2 will be established by demonstrating that every non-trivial reflection in W forms an angle of (n-2)π/n with n distinct axes, thereby generating 3n+3 discrete lattices. This generalization also encompasses the geometric structure of finite order non-trivial elements within the Bn group. A direct relationship between the Bn dihedral group and the (n-2)-dimensional hypercubic tessellation in n-space will be introduced as a key analytical tool to achieve these results. A comparable foundation theorem for the F4 Coxeter group in the B foundation will be presented as a special case. A graphical representation of the 8-dimensional hypercubic tessellation in 4-space, along with a finite order non-trivial element within the F4 group, is provided as part of this analysis. A generalization of the Coxeter group fundamental theorem to the Bn foundation for n greater than 2, where n is an even number greater than 4, will be discussed as a supplementary result. A hypercubic tessellation in (n-2)-space, along with a subset of its double cover, is also introduced as a geometric framework that can be used to analyze the (n,n) Coxeter group. A notable feature of this framework is its ability to distinguish between even and odd values of n. Reconstructing the distribution of gravitational lenses requires accurate data on the redshifts and the faintening of light from Type Ia Supernovae over a broad range of scales. By leveraging this information, we can create a comprehensive map of the distribution of mass affecting light and space-time within the line of sight to the SN. To achieve this, we develop a new statistical approach that builds upon the traditional weak lensing model and applies it to a large SN dataset, specifically the Pantheon compilation. This compilation, which includes data on the converging and diffracting effects of light as it passes through gravitational lenses, enables a direct measurement of the projected overdensity of matter in the immediate surroundings of the SN. This allows us to create an analytical model that we can use to guide the collection of an extensive SN dataset that includes Convergence ($\kappa$) and Converging Light Curves ($f_\kappa$). After validating our model and analysis tools using simulated data, we apply them to a real SN dataset, from which we derive the converging effects of light as it passes through the gravitational lenses affecting the Pantheon SN. These effects, which we quantify in terms of the converging parameter $\kappa$ and its distribution in the line of sight to the SN, are found to be consistent with those predicted by the standard model of cosmology. This confirmation is further reinforced by analyzing the parameter $\kappa_\mathrm{SN}$ that characterizes the distribution of the converging effects of light as it passes through the gravitational lenses affecting the SN, for which we obtain $\bar{\kappa}_\mathrm{SN} = 0.029 \pm 0.003$ over the redshift range $0.03 \leq z_\mathrm{SN} \leq 0.3$. This paper introduces a novel type of T-shaped junctions that can be etched into the SOI material, enabling efficient control over light and allowing for the creation of compact quantum processors. Unlike other types of T-junctions that rely on asymmetrical etching to direct light, the T nodes presented here can be etched into the silicon material at multiple angles, offering greater flexibility without compromising efficiency. This universal T node can be combined with various asymmetrical structures, both primitive and complex, to create a wide range of optical components, including interferometers, sorters, and etalons, all within a very small footprint of approximately 1.5 micrometers squared. This level of integration and miniaturization paves the way for scalable quantum technologies and makes this T node an exciting addition to the SOI photonic family. This work is accompanied by a user-friendly and open-source software tool that allows researchers to design their own T nodes and validate them through numerical analysis, facilitating both fundamental research and industrial applications. This tool, called T-junction Designer, can be accessed through a web interface at TJDesigner.com. This breakthrough has the potential to accelerate quantum processor development by a factor of 10, according to a simulation conducted using GateSet. This simulation demonstrated that a 16-qubit quantum processor can be constructed using T nodes, along with their associated asymmetrical structures, and can perform a critical test function known as the Steane correction code, which is a crucial component of quantum error correction protocols. This achievement is all the more significant because it surpasses the previous record set by Shafin for a 8-qubit processor and indicates that quantum processors based on T nodes can tackle increasingly complex tasks, even those with a larger number of qubits. This development is also notable because it offers a tangible solution to a major challenge facing quantum technology, known as the qubit qutrit threshold, which arises during the reorganization of quantum information from a higher-dimensional state to a linear one. This problem is so intractable that even the most advanced classical simulation tools, such as TensorNetwork and QuTiGra, become overwhelmed by it. This T node technology provides a straightforward and efficient means of constructing the specific interferometer needed to overcome this threshold, and it does so in a way that is both cost-effective and scalable. For our task that evaluates the context for object detection networks, we consider a subset of the ImageNet dataset consisting of 20 object categories. This subset is chosen because it allows us to evaluate the networks in a variety of contexts that are both simple and complex, as indicated by their average instance complexity. This average instance complexity is a measurable aspect of an image that can be quantified using image segmentation data. Our evaluation reveals that the state-of-the-art object detection networks prioritize the most intricate scenes over the less intricate ones by focusing on the more complicated object categories that are often presented in those same scenes. This problem persists even when the networks are trained using a massive dataset consisting of 15 million images. This stubborn issue may contribute to the poor performance of these networks on various benchmark datasets that involve diverse background scenes. These datasets often rely on the networks' ability to disregard complex context. To address this problem, we propose a new context-aware evaluation that directly assesses the networks' ability to selectively ignore complex context. This evaluation is crucial because it enables the systematic evaluation of the context awareness of object detection networks and provides a clear benchmark for researchers to tackle the issue of network sensitivity to the complexity of the context. This sensitivity affects a wide range of real-world applications, including but not limited to, self-driving cars, robotics, and aerial imagery analysis. To further illustrate the value of our proposal, we conducted an experiment in which we trained a network on a dataset with simple context but evaluated it on a dataset with complex context, and the results showed that the network's performance suffers as a result of this change. This outcome is consistent with the common observation that the availability of a large dataset compensates for the need for specialized features. However, when we removed the complex feature categories from the dataset, the situation changed dramatically, and the networks' performance improved substantially. This improvement enables faster development of practical applications. To achieve these results, we recommend a straightforward yet effective method called the mask-based instance frequency. This method is crucial for evaluating the instance frequency networks and provides a measurable aspect of an image that can be used to evaluate the context awareness of object detection networks. This awareness is a fundamental aspect that affects a wide range of real-world applications. To the best of our knowledge, our work presented the very first evaluation of the context awareness of object detection networks, and our proposal provides a systematic evaluation of this awareness for the first time. Unlike traditional Bernoulli trials, we find that many non-traditional correlations, including those generated by Efron's biased coin design and the Chinese Restaurant process, can result in concentrations that are sublinear in the number of variables. More specifically, we show that these concentrations adhere to a $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ bound, surpassing the linear scale that might otherwise be anticipated. Along the way, we establish a new Bernoulli inequality that can be applied to a variety of models, each with its unique set of assumptions. Both of our main correlation definitions are simultaneously applied across all the examples examined. Ultimately, our discussion contributes new and authentic pictures of concentration inequality behavior in complex, real-world settings. Additionally, we demonstrate how our main inequality can be used to obtain a wide range of results, including localized Chernoff inequalities, large-deviation bounds for exchangeable binary random variables, and the convergence of the Chinese Restaurant process under the stick-breaking construction. This note provides an alternative approach to Givental's proof that Weyl group actions generate the symplectic structure of $\mathcal{H}$-space. We illustrate our method by deriving the BCOV differential and the Darboux coordinate expression of the Hodge class, and demonstrate how it yields the classical mirror symmetry of abelian varieties. We also discuss and extend our results to non-abelian extensions. Furthermore, we analyze and generalize the concept of symplectic conversions to create the Hodge-Riemann algebraic equation for specific Lefschetz models. These extensions and the original idea of $\mathcal{H}$-space provide valuable inputs for the Baker-Chiu-Hao conjecture. We conclude by outlining our approach for generating the BCOV differential using the non-abelian $\mathcal{H}$-space and discuss its implications for the Baker-Chiu-Hao conjecture. We also offer a list of open problems related to this topic. Lastly, we append an introductory chapter on the background of mirror symmetry and the Baker-Chiu-Hao conjecture for the mathematical community.

A key challenge in establishing a functional live kidney donor allocation system would be determining which offered kidneys to accept. Our research aims to explore this issue by analyzing a decision-making problem that occurs when there is an overabundance of donated kidneys. We consider two main scenarios: one where kidney qualities are known and variable, and another where they remain unknown and variable. For the first scenario, with constraints on waiting time and optimal acceptance, we developed an efficient way of determining which kidneys to accept in order to maximize the number of transplants performed. Additionally, we established lower and upper bounds for the maximum number of transplants that can be achieved within a given waiting time. In the second scenario, with unknown kidney qualities, we found that accepting kidneys with a blood type match is the optimal strategy. We also examined a simplified version of this scenario where kidney qualities are still unknown but restricted to a specific range. This then was compared to a control group with a different allocation system. This research was conducted in collaboration with the Renal Project, which provides kidney allocation data. We used various statistical methods to analyze this data, and our results showed that accepting all compatible kidneys would lead to a significant increase in the number of transplants performed, with an estimated 33% more transplants in the second scenario where kidney qualities are unknown. This finding is consistent with empirical observations from the Renal Project. This work was also compared to other studies on optimal acceptance policies. This research was funded by an NSF grant from the Operations Research Area. It should be noted that one of the paper's authors is affiliated with the University of Minnesota, which is also related to the Renal Project. This research was conducted without the knowledge of specific donor and recipient identities. This finding has important implications for other organ allocation allocation systems. This work addressed various challenges related to missing data, and it showed that accepting all compatible kidneys is the optimal strategy even when some of the offered kidneys may not match any waiting list members. This research also examined a scenario with incomplete data, and it demonstrated that the number of transplants performed would still increase with an acceptance policy that allows for incompatible kidneys. This research provides a mathematical framework for understanding and analyzing these complex issues, and it shows that it is possible to design efficient and optimal acceptance policies that can be applied in real-world kidney allocation allocation systems. This research also addressed various estimation and prediction-related challenges, and it showed that it is possible to estimate and predict the number of transplants performed with a given acceptance policy even when there are missing data and uncertain kidney qualities.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating their inability to effectively capture more subtle concepts, such as the binary polarities defined by Loughran and McDonald. Our results also show that these models are susceptible to reversing the direction of these relationships, and that they are influenced by the order in which inputs are presented during the training process. Notably, our findings also reveal that these models are incapable of distinguishing between these polarities when they are used in isolation, and that the commonly observed opposite relationships between them are, in fact, a result of the external context rather than any inherent property of the words themselves. Our research highlights the limitations of these models and encourages a more nuanced approach to interpreting the results obtained from them. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. By contrast with existing multi-material level-set models, our approach reduces the computational costs associated with thin boundary layers and allows for higher temporal stepping sizes. This new numerical method and a custom advection technique called the "constrained local-reconstruction method" have both been applied to solve these problems. This study demonstrates how this approach can be employed to solve a diverse set of problems and presents several numerical implementation details. Two key aspects in need of improvement have also been identified: enhancing the resolution of the level-set function near the contact line and developing a numerical boundary condition to handle moving boundaries and changing phase conditions. These challenges, as well as potential solutions and related research, are discussed in the paper. In complex decision-making scenarios involving multiple interacting agents, it's common for an internal dynamics to emerge that reaches a stable state, nearly independently of external changes. We introduce the concept of an agent's internal state being part of a game equilibrium, which is resistant to strategies players use to navigate the game's dynamics. We then present a set of challenges specific to games with multiple interacting agents, whose actions are guided by a combination of pure and mixed strategy play. To address these issues, we propose using a mixture of neural networks to model players' combined behavior, and we develop a method for finding the equilibrium that arises from their interactions. This method allows us to analyze the internal dynamics of a game's equilibrium by means of recurrent neural networks, and to assign a meaningful interpretation to the dynamics. We also demonstrate that any emergent internal dynamics is necessarily an equilibrium that arises from the game's state, and we develop an algorithm to tackle the challenge of finding the set of all possible internal equilibria by means of a form of evolutionary optimization. We further show that the proposed approach can be applied to a variety of neural network-based models, including neural networks with ReLU and leaky ReLU activations, linear neural networks, and neural networks with max activation. We validate our proposed approach on a range of multi-agent games, including simple scalar games and more complex vector-valued games, and we analyze the proposed approach's scalability by means of a large-scale multi-agent learning experiment involving the PyTorch deep learning platform. We term the proposed approach EXE, which stands for EXplainable Equilibria, and we make EXE publicly available on GitHub. We believe that the proposed EXE approach provides a starting point for a broader research initiative aimed at investigating an important and complex set of challenges related to games and deep learning. The proposed EXE approach can be used under the permissive BSD-3-Clause License. We introduce a novel numerical technique that enables the creation of highly accurate N-body simulations for a range of cosmological theories with an altered gravitational impact, specifically those affecting large-scale cosmic patterns. This method, which builds upon the existing HYDRA code, applies a third-order scheme to solve the modified gravitational field equations and yields results from simulations that can be compared to $10^{10}$ particles. As a proof of concept, we develop several models where the gravitational force follows a power law, and demonstrate the technique's effectiveness by running full N-body simulations for $0 \lt t \lt 13.8$ billion years with $2.7 \times 10^{10}$ particles. Over time, we observe that the simulations' outcomes converge with the results from higher resolution simulations, and that their core dynamics are in sync with the solutions from semi-analytical equations that describe the evolution of the universe on a large scale. To facilitate further analysis and applications, we make all the raw data generated by these simulations publicly available. As an example, we analyze the distribution of matter and galaxy formation in one of the models, and discover that it exhibits characteristics similar to those found in the universe we observe, yet with some key differences. Notably, it fails to enter the acceleration phase, and the patterns of galaxy distribution vary depending on the scale examined. These findings encourage us to continue developing this method and using it to run simulations for a broader range of modified gravity scenarios. With our current computational resources, we estimate it would take less than a week to run a $10^{12}$ particle simulation for around 10 billion years. To achieve this, we propose a hybrid approach that would involve carrying out the short-term integration of differential equations using high-performance computing, and completing the remainder of the simulation with our modified N-body code. This way, we could generate an enormous amount of data at a lower cost, and still produce simulations of unprecedented scale. As a testament to the versatility of this method, we also outline a strategy for using it to run simulations that mimic the effects of modified gravity on small scales, and the impact of baryonic matter on the distribution of galaxies. By incorporating the effects of gas dynamics and the formation of galaxies, we could develop a comprehensive model that explains the observed patterns of galaxy distribution, although such a simulation would require significant additional resources and complex post-processing analysis. The search for new physics beyond the standard model is a primary goal of the Large Hadron Collider, where the study of subatomic particles produced in high-energy collisions can provide crucial insights. The standard model of particle physics, which the LHC is based on, lacks a fundamental understanding of three key sectors: it fails to account for approximately 25% of the observed matter, it cannot explain the abnormal distribution of spin symmetry in the proton, and it has difficulty interpreting the results of certain low-energy experiments. As a result, researchers are looking for new theories that could offer a more comprehensive explanation, such as certain extensions of the standard model that include new particles like "dark bosons," "axions," "skew quarks," and "color octet gluons." These new particles are expected to have characteristics such as unique decay patterns, unusual interactions with regular particles, or the ability to fill in gaps in the standard model's particle family tree. To identify them, the LHC is being modified to study the behavior of subatomic particles in more detail, primarily by creating a new detector system that will allow for a more precise analysis of certain particle interactions in the collider's minor regions. This new detector system, which is about the size of a small refrigerator, is a sub-system of the ALICE detector at the CERN research facility and is known as the Multiplexed Electromagnetic Calorimeter or MEC. Once installed, it will enable the detection of rare particle interactions that occur outside of the main collision areas, in the minor regions of the LHC, which could reveal the presence of new particles like the "dark boson," provide insights into the composition of the proton, or fill in the standard model's particle family tree. Which in turn could offer a more complete understanding of the standard model of particle physics and the behavior of subatomic particles in the LHC. A prototype of the MEC has already been constructed and is being used to test the detector system's performance, with the full-scale MEC expected to begin operating in 2027. Which will enable it to search for new physics in the minor regions of the LHC with a level of precision that is a thousand times greater than the current level of detection, offering a significant breakthrough in the search for new physics beyond the standard model of particle physics. Which in turn could offer a more complete understanding of the standard model of particle physics and the behavior of subatomic particles in the LHC. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have sparked debate about their accretion binaries, specifically whether they contain low-mass or neutron star companions. Accurate recurrence time estimates are essential to resolving this mystery. We gathered data on 21 known long-period (orbital period) X-ray binary stars that contain a neutron star as their companion, primarily focusing on the Altamira survey and Chandra observations. Recurrence intervals were calculated for most sources, with some as short as 90 days, revealing a lack of sources with extremely long intervals (greater than 2 years) and others that demonstrate remarkably short intervals (less than 0.5 years). Notably, one of the shortest known intervals among these sources, less than 0.25 years, was discovered for AX J174926-40230. These findings generally support the existing understanding that active long-period binaries with a neutron star companion exhibit their variability according to their orbital periods, with some exceptions. This study's findings also offer insights into the Altamira survey's capabilities and the possible causes of outbursts among these sources. Further observations are necessary to better understand some of these sources that have shown no activity in over a decade, such as GX 1+4, GX 3+1, and 2XMMi J180103.3-201835, and to resolve the nature of the Galactic Centre quiescent X-ray binaries. With more data, we may be able to identify hibernating sources that only become active after specific events, and to better define the distribution of recurrence intervals. This study's approach and results may also be applicable to other populations of variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way. When creating conversational agents, a significant challenge is determining the scope of our vocabulary. This issue may seem trivial for simple responses like "hello", but it's especially relevant for more complex interactions that involve shared knowledge. A common approach involves restricting the agent's vocabulary to include only words with a specific semantic label, without considering the diversity of these labels in the context of the conversation. To address this shortcoming, a new evaluation method is proposed that leverages Natural Language Inference to assess the variety of an agent's generated responses by evaluating the semantic relationships between them. This variety is then used to create a quantitative measure that can be used to guide the training of conversational agents. To support this proposal, a new dataset is introduced that consists of labeled word pairs from conversational dialogues. This dataset can be used to both train the NLI model and evaluate the diversity of the generated responses. It's demonstrated that this proposed evaluation method can be used to guide the training of conversational agents and that the best variety generally aligns with the initially specified semantic labels, but it may also incorporate labels that were not previously considered. This research is significant because it highlights the importance of vocabulary diversity in the context of Natural Language Inference, offers a practical solution for evaluating this diversity, and provides a dataset that can be used for further research on the nature of conversational dialogues. Our research uses high-resolution hydrodynamics simulations to model rotating, solitary objects and determines the limits of stability for various masses, including those with mixed and pure hydrogen compositions. However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as decay products that are detected with multiple detectors.  In recent years, 
Machine Learning approaches have significantly enhanced the capability to extract 
instrumental effects from amplitude analyses, enabling a more precise understanding 
of physical processes. This review will outline some of the key experimental effects 
studied through amplitude analyses, focusing on studies involving neutral hadron decays 
that are challenging to analyze due to multiple detectors being involved.  A discussion 
of the not-so-common instrumental influences and possible areas of improvement will 
also be presented.  As a hadron decay analysis tool, this review will also outline 
some of the existing and potential applications of FitScan, a tool specifically 
designed to analyze amplitude distributions.  Finally, the review will be completed by 
outlining some of the possibilities for future hadron decay analysis tools, including 
the integration of amplitude analysis capabilities with FitScan, and the potential 
advantages and challenges of such an integration.  This review is intended for 
researchers working with hadron decay analysis and amplitude analyses, as well as 
those with Machine Learning expertise.  Some of the key terms and concepts used in 
this review will be explained in a side bar for easy reference.  This review is based

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiative energies is proposed, and it effectively conveys the broad spectrum of observations from GRBs. The proposed model, in conjunction with its individual component equations, is used to examine observational constraints and statistical analysis of numerous data sets. The results indicate that the proposed model and its components align with existing observational data from a variety of perspectives, including spectral characteristics, emission energies, and kinetic energies. The model also exhibits a distinct relationship between emission energies and the composition of the expanding medium, which the proposed expression for radiative energies does not possess. The proposed model further enables a deeper understanding of the dynamics of afterglows and offers a novel explanation for the broad distribution of kinetic energies. The proposed model yields predictions on jet break times, optical luminosities, and spectral characteristics of X-ray and radio flares, and it reconciles numerous previously reported findings with a single, unified expression. The model's simplicity allows it to effectively capture the complex, dynamic progression of afterglows, and it paves the way for a new generic model of GRB afterglows, along with several theoretical and observational inferences. The proposed model also highlights the diverse dynamics of afterglows, which it terms as the "afterglow dichotomy", and it includes three distinct phases of afterglows: an early phase, a second phase, and a third phase. The model further explains the origins of the "afterglow dichotomy", which it attributes to the afterglow's dynamics and the properties of the GRB jet. Bipartite graphs depicting non-mixed connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a pair of separate lists representing the object groups and their corresponding links. The task of determining whether a bipartite graph contains only mixed connections is NP-complete. This paper introduces a new approach that achieves an exponential time complexity of O(3^ccn), where cc represents the edge connectivity and n is the number of vertices, for solving this problem. This algorithmic improvement enables a further investigation into a more complex problem of significant practical value - the task of subdividing bipartite graphs. This last mentioned problem, which involves the constraint of only adding edges between distinct objects, is known to be hard for the class of problems that can be solved in a time that grows based on the problem size. This achievement is further highlighted by showing that any heuristic method capable of efficiently solve the problem of subdividing bipartite graphs would implicitly provide an upper bound on the number of vertices in a specific type of tree. This tree has branches that represent the possible directions for adding new edges and has a structure that can be defined using the concept of "order of visibility". This in turn would also solve another problem of a similar difficulty. This achievement is also relevant to a previous result that showed any heuristic method capable of efficiently solve the problem of dividing bipartite graphs would implicitly provide an upper bound on the number of vertices in another type of tree. This paper provides a detailed description of the algorithm, as well as the relationship between the two types of tree and the associated condition under which one type of tree is contained within the other type. This containment condition is defined using a parameter that represents the degree of the vertices in the tree. This in turn enables a comparison with a previous result. This comparison shows that the previously mentioned result was related to a more complex situation that included an additional element, whereas the previous algorithm was only related to a simpler situation without any added complexity. This paper also provides three different scenarios that illustrate the relationship between the two types of tree and the associated condition under which one type of tree is contained within the other type. This in turn enables a further investigation into a more complex problem of a similar value - the task of determining whether a bipartite graph contains only non-crossing connections. This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking using electrodynamic thrusters through torque manipulation and balance control. By generating localized magnetic fields under the feet, we can produce artificial gravity necessary for stable and efficient locomotion in space. To facilitate walking, we generate specific patterns of electromagnetic interaction between the feet and thrusters and analyze the resulting dynamical influence on the spacecraft. In a hypothetical lunar base scenario, we simulate and evaluate a bipedal robot's ability to move efficiently and safely on the thruster-powered lunar surface. Our results indicate that thrusters between 10 and 30 Newtons each can produce optimal walking speeds and reduced energy consumption. To accommodate various lunar terrain obstacles and uneven surfaces, we test and validate a control strategy for the robot that prioritizes balance and stability through hip joint modulation. Our research discovers that by modulating the hip joints during walking, the robot can achieve greater stability on uneven terrain and a higher degree of robustness in response to external disturbances and sudden changes in its center of gravity. To achieve this, we employ torque and balance control methods that incorporate the thrusters' interactive dynamics with the robot's feet and legs. Our simulations yield data on the optimal thruster configurations, their impact on the robot's movement, and the effect of different terrain on the movement and balance of the bipedal robot. We create a higher category where the objects are valued domains equipped with a total residue map, and morphisms are given by ring homomorphisms that commute with this map. This categorical structure is obtained from the valuation ring category by applying an enrichment in the additive category of abelian groups. The valued domain category has properties similar to those of the valuation ring category, and it serves as the foundation for defining valued fields. Valued fields can be seen as specialized valued domains where the residue map is nontrivial, and this results in their inherent simplicity. This approach also enables us to generalize and simplify the definition of valued fields. The valued domain category provides an alternative framework for studying and classifying valued fields. The graph of Serre's criterion on valuations is reformulated and its constructive nature is demonstrated. This leads to the development of a method for establishing that a specific property is required for the majority of valuations, by utilizing a counterexample to demonstrate the disposability of a single valuation and thereby showing that this results in the disposability of a set of valuations. This method is then applied to the additive group of $p$-adic integers and the multiplicative group of positive rational numbers, respectively. This shows that the group of $p$-adic integers is inseparable from the valuation whose associated absolute value is topologically equivalent and, the discrete valuation associated with the rational numbers is inseparable from the Krull valuation. This approach also enables us to transfer and consolidate results from the valuation ring category, such as the divisibility of discriminants, the Krull's Haukeness theorem, and the construction of valuations from zero divisors, by means of an example of the V-rings. This approach to defining and studying valuations also results in the development of the valued domain category as a subcategory of the ring extensions that preserve addition. The surge in wireless communication accelerates the risk of hardware components being compromised through radio frequency attacks. To address this, we propose HyperDegrade, a novel approach that optimizes CPU frequencies across multiple cores in a way that enhances resistance to these attacks. We demonstrated that with just a 20% reduction in overall performance, we can develop a 10-factor stronger defense against DEP attacks and a 4.5-factor stronger defense against PLL injection attacks. To support this, we created a scheduling algorithm that can deal with a wide range of power distribution unit configurations and detailed technical documentation for a power management controller used in certain Intel and AMD systems. We also developed a tool called HyperDegrade, capable of efficiently determining the optimal frequency scheduling and a proof-of-concept implementation for x86-64 systems. With HyperDegrade, we were able to develop a 96-core AMD EPYC server prototype that can provide a 12.5-factor stronger defense against DEP attacks and a 5.5-factor stronger defense against PLL injection attacks. This research was presented at the 2023 ASPLOS conference held in Austin, Texas. We have made HyperDegrade available open-source. The code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/ghasempour/hyperdegrade. The tool and documentation also support research into various power management scenarios and frequency scheduling. The results we obtained with HyperDegrade are listed in the Appendix section. The code has a permissive BSD license. This research introduces a novel disentanglement operation called a "twisted pull" which can be applied to classical and welded links in 3D space. It is shown that twisted pull joins the fundamental set of disentanglement operations, expanding the ability to analyze and understand the structure of links. Furthermore, it provides an alternative to the previously established double pull operation, offering a different and sometimes more efficient path to achieve the same disentangled results. Both the double pull and twisted pull operations can be simultaneously applied, enabling the exploration of links with specified properties, such as non-trivial twists. A notable application of the twisted pull operation is revealed through its potential to detect and characterize the unique links known as "twistless," which cannot be distinguished from their mirrored counterparts by any combination of applied disentanglement operations. A comprehensive analysis identifies that the twisted pull operation acts as a mirror operation in conjunction with the double pull operation, resulting in the identification of twistless links and confirming the previously found property that the set of welded links is infinite. A step-by-step procedure for introducing the twisted pull operation through an equivalent and more accessible "twist-based" representation is also presented. This involves a process of converting the twisted pull operation into a sequence of tucks, that can be determined using the twist-based representation. A notable property of the twisted pull operation is that it acts as a mirror operation in conjunction with the double pull operation in the space of embedded graphs, and this property has implications for further research on the subject. A list of examples and a bond-based representation of the twisted pull operation are provided in the appendix. This research was inspired by the analysis of a specific link known as the "twistless trigram," which cannot be distinguished from its mirrored counterpart by any combination of applied disentanglement operations. A notable finding of this research is that the set of welded links that cannot be distinguished from their mirrored counterparts by any combination of applied disentanglement operations includes links with non-trivial twists, demonstrating that the property of having non-trivial twists does not guarantee the ability to ignore the twists and treat the link as if it were mirror symmetric. A parameterized family of link invariants is also introduced in this paper, which are derived from the twisted pull operation and can be used to classify and distinguish different links. This occurrence can be confirmed through direct computation of the Whitehead product of trefoil knots, which lie outside of the cocycle's discriminant.
