Research on intricate systems often uncovers hidden patterns when raw data is directly analyzed, yet the true geometry and underlying causes frequently remain obscure. Our investigation utilizes an innovative hybrid approach that combines conventional methods with a novel algorithm to reveal the concealed structure and mechanisms driving dynamics in complex networks. As a test case, we examine a particular nanoscale system where interactions between adjacent pairs of spins cause magnetic reversal, and our findings show that the assembly's spatial geometry and the type of interactions influencing the spin interactions are crucial for controlling reversal patterns. Specifically, we discover that the assembly's curvature and the distribution of triangle-based interactions with the ability to form closure triangles with the assembly's boundaries play a critical role in determining the reversal patterns. By integrating the algorithm with numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the interplay between the interactions within pairs and triangles ultimately dictates the reversal patterns and provide a roadmap for similar future studies on other complex systems. This research offers a versatile and adaptable framework that can be applied to a broad range of complex systems, from nanoscale spin systems to large-scale networked systems in biology, finance, and transportation, among others. We studied observations from the Solar Wind Electrodynamics Investigation - Radio Frequency unit on board Parker Solar Probe to understand the solar wind energy flux within the inner heliosphere. Analyzing data from 25 degrees to 187 degrees sunward of the sun's center, we found that the energy flux in the solar wind breeze is highest at lower sunward angles and follows the expected shape of a parabola as predicted by the solar wind model that takes into account the outflow of solar energy and mass from the sun's corona and surface. This increase in energy flux at smaller sunward angles is particularly notable and may be attributed to the energy input from solar jets and magnetically active regions in the sun's photosphere and corona. This effect becomes more apparent at larger sunward angles when considering observations from the Sun's southern hemisphere, indicating a possible hemispheric asymmetry. This study's findings highlight the significance of data from Parker Solar Probe in the inner heliosphere and the insights they provide into the solar wind, the sun's energy and mass outflow, and the energy and angular momentum that the sun loses over time. This knowledge can be used in the development of new solar wind models that can be tested and then used to understand solar wind dynamics and the effects it has on the angular momentum of the sun. This study introduces a novel type of non-abelian "ether" term, which is a topological Chern-Simons coefficient, in non-abelian gauge theories, specifically in $SU(2)$ and $SU(3)$ Yang-Mills models. When combined with the Weyl semimetals' linear-surface-termination condition, the non-abelian "ether" term leads to robust, three-fold degenerate zero-energetic points in all three directions within a three-dimensional cubic lattice. The non-abelian "ether" term's impact is analyzed at finite temperatures using thermal and momentum-space renormalization group methods, demonstrating that the non-abelian "ether" term's effect on the energy spectrum and critical behavior near these points is remarkably insensitive to temperature variations. This relative stability of the points' energy spectra and critical behavior to temperature changes differentiates non-abelian "ether" terms from other topological terms, such as the Weyl semimetals' $\kappa$-term introduced earlier, which is shown to exhibit much greater temperature dependence. All-in-all, this study reveals non-abelian "ether" terms to be highly versatile, capable of producing multiple isolated points of zero energy within a three-dimensional lattice, and these results pave the way for exploring these terms in three-dimensional lattices with multiple isolated points in both zero and finite temperature regimes. This includes a discussion of realization possibilities using cold atomic or optical lattices. A dedicated appendix is provided which outlines a more general non-abelian "ether" term capable of describing multiple isolated points in both zero and finite energy regimes along with an analysis of its low-energy effective action. In accelerators, knowing the position and shape of particle beams is crucial for ensuring reliability and efficiency. To this end, a method is proposed that leverages the vertical motion of charged particles as they traverse a horizontally-focused gun in a wakefield accelerator. As particles move vertically, they experience a changing electric field and thus travel at varying distances horizontal to the gun. When these particles are imaged on a screen, the resulting pattern can be analyzed to determine the beam's distribution and whether it's focused or not. This method is particularly beneficial because it doesn't require any additional equipment beyond a standard gun and a screen, making it a cost-effective and real-time solution for beam diagnostics that can be applied to accelerators of any size. A proposed experiment using an s-band gun at the Brookhaven National Laboratory's Accelerator Test Facility is also presented. This research has the potential to advance our understanding of the behavior of beams in accelerators and the development of new scanning technologies that could be used in various applications, including medical procedures. The limitations and biases of instruments can significantly impact the interpretation of data and correct for them, we need a comprehensive understanding of how they affect the observed signal. The s4cmb Python package is designed to simulate these effects on CMB maps, specifically for spatial and polarisation variations, and can also incorporate realistic noise levels. The code can generate maps that reflect the instrumental response of future experiments, such as the Simons Observatory, the COrE satellite and the LiteBURST experiment. The focus of LiteBURST instrumentation simulation is unique in that it primarily detects and analyzes scalar particles through annihilation signals rather than traditional CMB fluctuations. The package enables users to input various models of the CMB signal, including power spectra and foreground maps, and then applies the instrumental response and noise to the maps, facilitating an in-depth analysis of systematics and their impact on future experiments. The simulation of LiteBURST instrumentation takes a different approach in that it primarily detects and analyzes scalar particles through annihilation signals rather than traditional CMB fluctuations. The code takes into account various systematics and noise sources, such as correlated noise, beam asymmetry, Ali-Mantiello effect, half-wavelength aliasing, detector non-linearity and more, all of which are critical for an accurate interpretation of future CMB data. The simulation of the CMB signal and noise is accessible through the package's command line interface or through Python scripting. The results of the simulations are presented in the form of CMB maps, power spectra and bias estimates, all of which are critical for designing and analyzing future CMB experiments. In this study, we systematically substitute different components of BART in task arrangements of 12-letter words, using a dataset provided by McCauley and Hare (2020). We discover that the initial training of BART prioritizes semantic understanding over lexical arrangement. When considering generation components, we find that both the generator and the mask generator play crucial roles in achieving high arrangement accuracy. By analyzing the performance of BART in arranging words from the same part of speech but with different meanings, we identify a significant contradiction in its design that may hinder its ability to comprehend local syntax. We conclude that both the design of models and the evaluation methods may need adjustment if pre-trained language models are to be effectively employed in tasks that involve the arrangement of words in specific local contexts. We suggest possible modifications, including a new evaluation metric that assesses the arrangement of words with the same semantic value. With the inclusion of a task that arranges words from the same part of speech but with different meanings, our dataset now consists of seven tasks that can be used for further research. We make our dataset publicly available. We hope this study and our dataset may contribute to the development of both language models and evaluation methods that are more adept at handling the complex local syntax of natural language. We discuss the implications of our findings for current approaches to natural language generation and the evaluation of transformer-based models. This paper establishes links between algebraic geometry and number theory to create upper limit functions for successive minima of rational functions over algebraic curves defined by polynomial equations with coefficients in a number field. These limit functions are constructed using Ramshaw's method and certify the non-existence of specific geometric configurations in roots of the curves. As a result, we obtain lower bound estimates for these minima, expressed in terms of coefficients of the curve and its derivatives. Eventually, we connect these estimates to the second main theorem of Diophantine approximation theory. Specifically, we show that there are positive constants that allow us to bound below the number of times a non-constant rational function can be differentiated before its coefficients become integers. Examples are provided to demonstrate the simplicity and generality of these constant functions. Furthermore, we establish connections between these constant functions and previous estimates based on another, different approach used by Viola. Additionally, we derive comparable estimates for another, distinct concept called the Abelian integral's lower bound, which, in turn, enables us to estimate the number of times a function can be successively integrated before its coefficients become integers. Finally, we outline a strategy for further improving these constant functions, thereby potentially expanding the results to more general and complex settings. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have scrutinized 19 newly proposed globular clusters located in the galaxy's bulge and situated at a low galactic latitude. Using data from the $K_s$-band depth of the VVV survey, we calculated the photometry for these potential clusters and compared it to their observed properties. If a linear correlation holds, the mean and standard deviation of the photometry should align with established values for the galaxy's bulge and the specific VVV filter used. We rejected nine candidates whose photometric data did not fit this expectation and were likely misidentified. We also calculated the two-color index for the remaining ten clusters and found that they fall within the known parameter ranges for the galaxy's bulge. We then analyzed the proper motions of these ten clusters and removed three with values that did not match the general pattern of the galaxy's bulge. We are left with seven clusters whose properties are similar to those found in the galaxy's bulge but we cannot determine their specific location. We recommend observing these seven clusters with a spectrograph to confirm their nature and gain a better understanding of their chemical composition. We have made the data for these seven clusters available and encourage further analysis. A note has been added regarding the inclusion of a zero-point correction for the proper motions calculated using the TGAS and VVV data. In 2019, the "Hyper-Invariant MERA" proposal emerged as a holographic neural network architecture, capable of achieving superposition states and executing quantum computations on entangled networks, while resisting changes in various parameters. This research expands upon that concept by introducing a new, approximate version of the architecture, dubbed the "Hyper-Invariant Approximate MERA" (HIAMERA), which maintains the ability to simulate a vast array of models and resist changes in various parameters. Unlike its precise hyper-invariant counterpart, HIAMERA allows for the execution of short-lived, approximate quantum computations on networks with power-law dependencies and enables state manipulation through the erasure channel, making it an error-correcting code capable of protecting a limited amount of information within a vast entangled network. This proposal can be viewed as a hybrid of the HaPPY and TN Holographic Renormalization approaches. HIAMERA's advantages are demonstrated through applications to the simulation of certain models and the execution of a specific quantum computation. This research introduces multiple metrics for evaluating the performance of HIAMERA and explores the relationship between its parameters and the executed computations. Ultimately, this work offers a practical and efficient, approximately holographic neural network architecture tailored for the simulation of power-law dependent models and the execution of the quantum computation associated with the erasure channel. This proposal holds promise for broadening the scope of holographic neural networks to an exponentially larger set of applications. This research is accompanied by publicly accessible code. Given the approximately holographic nature of this architecture, it is reasonable to ask whether HIAMERA can be viewed as a specific, hybrid version of the HaPPY and TN Holographic Renormalization approaches, capable of executing a specific quantum computation on power-law dependent networks, and if so, what guidelines can be established for its use, such as the development of HIAMERA's optimal parameter maps? Additionally, this work leaves numerous open research directions, including the investigation of HIAMERA's relationship to the HaPPY and TN Holographic Renormalization approaches, the execution of various quantum computations on power-law dependent networks, the analysis of HIAMERA's performance through alternative metrics, and the exploration of its applications to an even broader set of models. This paper is accompanied by one appendix. This research was funded by the University of Connecticut. Although these techniques offer significant advantages over traditional approaches, there are concerns about overfitting due to limited training data, typical in process-centric contexts. Additionally, processes often exhibit fluctuations over time, another challenge these methods often fail to address. In response to these issues, our research explores alternative deep-learning techniques that prioritize model simplicity and effectiveness, while also introducing a set of pre-trained deep learning models that can capture patterns across different processes and reduce time-dependent variations. Thomson scattering off electrons is a significant process in solar flares, particularly in the near-ultraviolet range, and is typically modeled using a Boltzmann distribution to approximate the electron energy. This research utilizes numerical simulations of electron interactions to directly generate continuum spectra in the near-Ultraviolet, as demonstrated with the 1985 solar flare data from AD Leo, by accurately recreating the emitted spectra through a superposition of narrow Gaussian distributions that mirror the true electron energy distributions. This approach yields a better fit to the observed spectra, with a chi-squared value per degree of freedom that is significantly lower than previous models that relied on a Boltzmann distribution. This new method in particular highlights the importance of accurate electron energy distributions in modeling continuum spectra. This approach may also be applicable to stellar atmospheres beyond the near-Ultraviolet solar flares presented here. This work is an expansion upon our previous study of the 1998 September 4th solar flare from RS Cran, which showed that electron energy distributions are crucial for accurately modeling continuum spectra in the near-Ultraviolet. In recent years, point cloud models have gained significant traction due to their ability to process sensitive information, such as 3D faces and bodies, without the need for preprocessing. However, these models are vulnerable to producing unwanted and potentially harmful transformations, which can compromise privacy. Currently available methods fail to adequately address this issue, particularly in scenarios where high-fidelity reconstruction is necessary. Our solution addresses this challenge by introducing a new smoothing technique, tailored for point cloud models, which prevents the model from producing excessive stretching and folding. In contrast to methods that rely on learned components, our technique is efficient, primally weighted, and $10\times$ faster than its alternatives. Furthermore, it surpasses existing approaches in quality and accuracy according to the FSD score and the normal-based metric. Our technique also offers a significant improvement in privacy preservation for 3D face generation models. With its optimized design, our solution is suitable for various applications, including but not limited to 3D face and body analysis, where low-resolution, sensitive data must be handled. Our code is available at https://github.com/PhD-DJ/TPC.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been developed to extract eigenenergies from photoresponse spectra in the complex energy plane. The RPA + Jost method allows for a precise analysis of the structure and dynamics of the nuclear many-body system. A recent study employed this method to examine the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O, revealing a intricate pattern of energy and width beneath the main resonance peak. Contrary to traditional views, the $^{16}$O is not represented by a single resonance state but instead comprises multiple states with distinct properties, and the width of these states exhibits significant variability. These findings demonstrate the capability of the RPA + Jost method in uncovering intricate information about the dynamics of the system and provide new insights into the internal workings of $^{16}$O. The developed framework and the outcomes of this study are applicable to the study of other electric multipoles and other systems, such as light nuclei and finite matter. The interconnection with three-body force and the complexity of the density fluctuations of the system in one-body space are also discussed. The developed code is available upon request. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect clusters in dynamic systems by defining an impact distance that accounts for both spatial and temporal differences between data points. This method demonstrates superior performance in identifying latent structures within dynamic systems, as compared to conventional techniques such as PCA, k-means, and DBSCAN. Notably, the proposed approach yields results that align with established physical models, including the Roessler circuit and a percolation model, as well as synthetic and real-world data, showcasing its broad applicability. Developing a neural language modeling adversarial game that scales to large vocabularies has been a persistent challenge. Limitations in model size constrain the vocabulary generativity, leading to models that poorly predict rare words. Current methods to enhance vocabulary size are either resource-intensive or inefficient in word predictions. We present SparseGAN, a system that efficiently handles large vocabularies and our experiments show it outperforms existing approaches. For a vocabulary of 89K words, SparseGAN achieves the state-of-the-art Inference Time and Word Prediction Accuracy compared to conventional adversarial techniques, Generative Adversative Trainers, and sparse models including SparseNLLF and Adam-Sparse. The theory of interstellar panspermia suggests that life could be transferred from one star system to another through microbial means, potentially allowing life to thrive beyond its initial origin. Although this concept is intellectually alluring, verifying this hypothesis is a significant scientific challenge. To that end, we are exploring methods to confirm the reality of interstellar panspermia by analyzing data from existing and future radio telescopes focusing on signal patterns that could indicate the presence of biological matter in space. Animal movement plays a significant role in the dynamics of ecosystems and can be significantly influenced by a creature's preference for resources as well as specific individual characteristics. Implementing models that accurately account for these preferences and individual traits at a population level, especially for species with wide-spread distributions, presents a major challenge. Our research introduces a novel statistical method that incorporates Mark-Recapture theory with spatial statistics to estimate individual-level resource choice and spatial mobility patterns. We apply and test this method using data from radio-tracking European roe deer. Our results show that this method effectively recovers individual-specific parameters for both resource choice and mobility, reducing bias associated with other methods. We also find that this approach can differentiate between the effects of resource choice and other individual traits on a creature's spatial distribution. Ultimately, our method provides a valuable tool for biologists studying large, dispersed animal populations. Our code is available online. We discuss the method's potential applications and suggest possible modifications to make it more efficient. Additionally, we examine the method's potential to model seasonal changes in resource choice and mobility. Lastly, we explore and reject the hypothesis that the pattern of deer's habitat selection observed in this study can be explained by birth or mortality events. Our findings have significant implications for how we model the dynamics of populations and provide new insights into the migratory patterns of European roe deer. Our research also sheds light on the statistical challenges of analyzing capture-recapture data from species with complex spatial distributions and offers a novel perspective on the debate surrounding individual versus population-level resource choice. We find that mobility among deer is influenced by their preference for specific resources and that this preference changes seasonally. Unlike conventional approaches that assume differentiability of elasticity with respect to stretch, we establish an existence and uniqueness result for solutions of the elastic flow equation under the weakened assumption that elasticity exhibits Carathéodory differentiability with respect to stretch. This method's advantage becomes apparent during system development life cycles' verification phase, where it offers significant benefits. Our approach is not a replacement for conventional techniques but rather a complementary tool for both developers and testing teams. In this research, we develop reliable and robust algorithms for both unidirectional and bidirectional network age estimation, even when the network contains a small number of malicious nodes. Our primary assumption is that the network follows a random false name model and consists of a small world structure, with a central hub and individual clusters that are only partially connected. We achieve our results by utilizing a randomized consensus algorithm and implementing a decentralized, robust estimation technique. Our key contributions are a unidirectional network age estimation algorithm and a bidirectional algorithm, both with a linear distance cost and robustness against a large number of malicious nodes. We also explore and examine various variants and our results demonstrate that our algorithms are highly efficient and effective in small world networks. In contrast, bidirectional estimation allows the network to reach a much higher level of scalability. In simulations of numerical relativity with Einstein's theory of gravity, generating an appropriate set of initial data that satisfies both the Einstein field equations and the boundary conditions of a computational model has consistently posed a problem. A significant portion of research focuses on the conformally flat approach; however, this method often encounters issues when used to simulate scenarios involving rotating black holes. A new method we call "CTTK" builds upon Chru'siel and Retzch's work and employs a direct solver to address the issues with the conformally flat approach. By bypassing the need to combine analytical and numerical solutions, "CTTK" allows for the direct resolution of conformal singularities. This method has been successfully applied to the simulation of rotating black holes and our results show that it can accurately reproduce the same outcomes as "CaGa" methods. Notably, "CTTK" is capable of generating initial data for rotating black holes with their magnetic dipole moment set to zero, a feature that has not been previously achieved through numerical relativity. This achievement is made possible by the introduction of a new "rotational" gauge that helps eliminate conformal singularities and not all of the previously used parameters are independently variable. This includes the black hole's mass, the rotational parameter, and the magnetic dipole moment. This reduction in variables further simplifies the simulation and makes it even more comparable to real-world scenarios. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized scientific interest and pinpointed the Sirigiri's point (with an anomalous Hall angle of $\theta_H=90^\circ$) as a crucial phenomenon to understand and manipulate. Understanding and controlling this phenomenon are hindered by the lack of experimental data on the Anomalous Nernst Effect (ANE) and the Hall angle in magnetic thin films. Our study fills this gap by measuring the Anomalous Nernst Coefficient ($S_{xy}$) and Hall angle ($\theta_H$) in 2 unit cells thick Mn$_3$NiN films, demonstrating an extremely small Hall angle of $7.7^\circ$ and an anomalous Nernst angle of $89.3^\circ$, indicating a nearly perfect Sirigiri's point and minimal side switching in magnetic hystereses, likely resulting from the films' ultra-thin thickness and the absence of surface anisotropic magnetism. These unique features of the Anomalous Nernst Effect in these films offer promising prospects for controlling the Anomalous Hall Effect in ultra-thin magnetic materials. Moreover, we propose an analytical model for the Anomalous Nernst Effect in magnetic thin films and Sirigiri's point. Lastly, our findings and model predictions highlight the Sirigiri's point as a stable state in a broad range of temperatures and magnetic moments, distinguishing it from previous misconceptions and identifying it as a non-trivial and exotic magnetic state that lies on the border of multiple magnetic phases induced by competition and interface anisotropic magnetism. This state can be either a canted antiferromagnetic or a ferrimagnetic state, depending on the films' thickness, temperature, and interface anisotropic magnetism. This discovery and our proposed model for the Anomalous Nernst Effect in magnetic thin films and Sirigiri's point provide a framework for understanding and controlling the Anomalous Hall Effect in ultra-thin magnetic materials, which have vast potential for applications in the manipulation and control of the Anomalous Nernst Effect and the Sirigiri's point. This could enable the realization of a non-reciprocal, magnetic field modulation of the Anomalous Nernst Effect and the Sirigiri's point, as well as the demonstration of non-reciprocal, planar thermal and charge transport in magnetic thin films and Sirigiri's point. The basic concept of "elementary intelligence," which suggests that simpler components can give rise to sophisticated global behavior when working together, has been a recurring theme in mathematics and computing. This ideology is reflected in the "less clever elements, more intelligent whole" mantra. To explore this notion, we examine a diverse set of computational models, each with its unique characteristics, and discuss their capacity to exhibit "intelligent" group-level properties. This journey through complex systems from science and technology takes a more critical look at the relationship between the simplicity of individual elements and the advanced global intelligence they can display. By delving into examples like neural networks, cellular automata, genetic algorithms, and social network dynamics, we investigate the intricate interplay between the components' complexity and their collective global expression. Along the way, we also consider alternative, and sometimes contradictory, perspectives on the interplay between the simplicity of elements and the sophistication of their global expression. Ultimately, this study aims to provide a comprehensive and in-depth examination of the diverse ways in which global intelligence can manifest through the interconnection of individual elements, and the various ways these elements can be defined and understood. By exploring and presenting a broad range of computational models and their capacity for complex global behavior, we hope to contribute to the ongoing discussion and analysis of the intricate relationship between the components of a system and its overall global expression. This work introduces a tensor framework for a Euclidean space of any dimension, where geometric tensors define the space's properties and serve as the fundamental elements in the space. Every element in the space can be represented as a linear combination of the basis geometric tensors, with coefficients that make up the coordinate system for the space. This tensor approach is particularly useful as it allows for the differentiation between absolute and relative (or artificial) geometric properties of a space. A key aspect of this model is the ability to determine geometric tensors from the metric tensor that defines the space, using the geometric tensors as the basis. This is made possible through a decomposition method that can be derived using either the Euler-Poisson or the Hamilton-O'Hough equations, depending on the specific situation. This tensor framework has been successfully applied in various research and theoretical physics settings. All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and encompass each of its three variants through a specific realization of the Virasoro algebra. Within these theories, a distinct set of operators, known as Ward, forms a commutative collection that arises from the conformal algebra's central extension. For the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda theory, we have discovered multiple Ward relationships that characterize how the operators' ordering affects their conformal properties, going beyond the knowledge that currently exists for this model. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that its operators' ordering can be rearranged in a specific manner, each of which is associated with a distinct $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Lie algebra root. This ordering is so crucial that it enables a root system-based classification of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda theory's operators. Notably, only certain of these operators possess the property of primary convergence, which is essential for performing loop regularizations in correlators calculations. Consequently, the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda theory's correlators' analytically continued expressions can be obtained using a different approach than the Bethe ansatz, which primarily targets the space of solutions that are physically valid. These results also imply that the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda theory's operators' collections are infinite in number, in contrast to the finite nature of those in the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Lie algebra-based Toda models. Moreover, we have discovered an intricate relationship between the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda theory's operators, namely that they can be matched one-to-one with the operators from the Liouville theory, although this pairing is dependent on the operators' ordering. This unique pairing of operators provides the foundation for developing two-particle interaction formulas within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda theory. Lastly, for the purposes of cosmological applications, we have analytically extended the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda theory's two-particle interaction formulas, which allows correlators calculations that involve the conformal field theory's quantum gravity-related parameter, known as $\gamma$. These analyses demonstrate that the validity of these analyses is limited to a specific range of $\gamma$, which can be determined by examining the properties of the operators' ordering. A Decoding Approach for Behind-View Observations Developed from Electrocorticogram Signals during Overground Walking in a Paraplegic Subject with an Spinal Cord Injury is Outlined.  In order to regain mobility and independence, regenerative spinal cord treatments or exoskeletal solutions for paraplegic patients require the ability to accurately monitor and understand their natural gait patterns.  Although visual observations are a straightforward method for this purpose, they have the disadvantage of being a forward-facing activity that can be cumbersome for the subject to perform while walking, even with the support of a walker.  Therefore, a previous study was conducted with a paraplegic patient who is able to control their hand movements with their brain activity, allowing them to walk behind an observation window and press a button to mark the moment they take a step.  From these recordings, a previous study was able to create a decoding approach that could determine the start and end of a step from the brain activity, but did not examine the underlying factors that influence these decisions.  In our current research, we were able to clarify the features that the decoder is identifying, and found that it is pinpointing the moment when the foot begins to move, but not the moment when the foot touches the ground.  Additionally, we found out that the progression of the brain activity during a step is linear, but not uniform, and this information can be utilized in further developments such as restoring sensory functions, promoting muscle contractions, or modulating the neural control that guides the gait.  Moreover, our analysis enables the use of these signals in a closed-loop system that could influence the brain activity, and thus the movement of the feet, through feedback from the observation of the gait.  This kind of system could feed it with information about the movement of the feet, obtained from the observations, and it could use this information to update the state that the decoder is using to predict the start and end of a step, allowing it to move forward even in the presence of any delays.  In order to demonstrate this capability, we developed a new feature that is based on the time it takes to complete a step, and showed that it and the previously defined features are sufficient to create a decoder that can determine the start and end of a step, even in the presence of any noise or variations in the gait pattern.  This decoder uses an algorithm that is able to update the state that it uses to predict the start and end of a step based on the observations of the gait

We demonstrate that any finite index subgroup of $G$ containing a non-degenerately embedded copy of $H$ can be constructed from $H$ through a sequence of vertex splits of the graph defining $G$. This confirms a conjecture of Minnozzi and the first author, initially proposed in 2017. This proof relies on a new inductive property of right-angled Artin complexes characterized by their vertex splitting behavior. As a result, we obtain a generalized version of the famous group minimality property of random graph groups discovered by Fowler. This leads to the conclusion that many groups defined by specific graphs are of type $\WR$, which in turn implies their word and group generating series coincide. Identifying connections between elements in complex systems, especially dynamic systems, is crucial for understanding where interactions lie. A new method called DDECE (Deep Dynamic Efficient Connectivity Estimation) uses variational autoencoders to pinpoint connections, differentiating them from internal representations, and trains a reservoir computing model to determine dynamic connections, all while accounting for noise. A key feature of DDECE is it determines the connectivity as it changes over time, offering a rich overview of the system's evolution. To demonstrate the effectiveness of DDECE, it's applied to multiple synthetic systems and real-world data, including EEG recordings from a seizure, which visualized as a movie shows a step-by-step disintegration of the connection between elements as a seizure takes hold. DDECE's performance in detecting changes in connectivity is comparable to other state-of-the-art methods, all while outperforming them in efficiency. The code for DDECE is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/brainbowteam/DDECE. The project is also accompanied by a web application that allows for interactive exploration of the results obtained with DDECE, accessible at https://ddece.brainbow.tech/. The findings presented in this study are validated by experts in the field of neurology. The development of DDECE paves the way for a new generation of efficient methods for discovering and analyzing the dynamic connections in complex systems, enabled by the use of reservoir computing and variational autoencoders. The code for DDECE has been successfully applied to a wide range of time series data, including genetic data that changes over time, EEG recordings from the brain during the onset of seizures, and stock market data, among others, as seen in the results presented in the supplementary materials. This research identifies biological motion patterns in video footage. Biological motion occurs when the movement of multiple non-rigid objects, such as humans, follows an organic path, in contrast to random movements of individual components, in this case, limbs. We developed an automated method to pinpoint the source of biological movement within a given video. This source is considered the primary focus of the viewer and is often the center of attention in still images and videos featuring multiple moving subjects, including humans and some animals. Our approach starts by extracting and representing local features from each frame of the video. A 2D grid representing an organism's body is then superimposed over these features. We calculated the direction of each feature's movement in relation to the video frame's temporal changes. This information is used to determine the probability that a particular feature constitutes a limb of the organism in question. In the end, we defined the organism as the collection of limbs that demonstrate non-random movement patterns. We tested and validated our approach using a custom-made dataset consisting of various biological and non-biological movement patterns, in addition to well-known biological subjects like humans and some animals, as well as some less conventional organisms like fungi and plants. We also provided numerical and visual analysis of these results. Our approach has numerous potential applications, including but not limited to, segmentation of complex videos, focus of attention in still images and videos, and modeling the physical body of the organism in question. We have made our dataset available to the public as a valuable resource for further development and testing of our approach, as well as other related research. This dataset can be found at https://github.com/Amir-Paneri/Biological-Motion-Detection-Code. We have also made the code for our approach available at the same location. The underlying structure of the Coppersmith-Winograd (CW) algorithm from 1971, known for achieving near-optimal matrix multiplication efficiency, has been leveraged to develop the Broadband algorithm in 2012. Building upon this foundation, researchers have successfully created a modified version of the algorithm known as Broadband' (BRD), which exhibits optimal scalar complexity. Nonetheless, the complexity of the CW algorithm surpasses the square root boundary that is efficiently breakable using the fast Fourier transform, resulting in an impediment for matrices of higher dimensions. Our novel contribution introduces a 7th order version of the Broadband' algorithm (denoted as 7BRD), which efficiently breaks down 513x513 matrix arrays into smaller components, comparing favorably to the existing state of the art, particularly when executing on Graphics Processing Units. The analytical findings presented in our research, accompanied by comprehensive numerical testing, form the basis of our subsequent discussions. The numerical analysis, conducted using a single NVIDIA V100 GPU, reveals that the 7BRD algorithm delivers superior performance to the premier state-of-the-art matrix inversion methods, including Pott's 9x9 and Beyer's 17x17, for a wide range of matrix dimensions including those of significant practical importance, such as 4095x4095. The numerical results presented in our study demonstrate the potential of higher order fast matrix inversion algorithms in real-world applications, and the 7BRD algorithm is set to become the standard reference for future research in this domain. The 7BRD code developed during our research has been designed with modularity in mind, allowing for easy addition of new higher order matrix inversion algorithms, and is available for download on GitHub. The numerical analysis presented in our study showcases the implications of using the 7BRD algorithm on real-world problems, including the solution of large nonlinear systems of equations and the calculation of Gram matrices in Gaussian process regression, as well as the performance obtained on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU, which amounts to a scalar complexity of approximately 22910, achieved for a 4095x4095 matrix array. The 7BRD algorithm has the potential to deliver the best performance on a wide range of matrix dimensions, extending well into the thousands, and demonstrates the potential of the hybrid approach used in its design, which combines the benefits of both divide-and-conquer and fast Fourier transform-based matrix inversion algorithms. The code developed during our research includes multiple variants of the 7BRD algorithm, each optimized for a different set

This research introduces topological Anderson conductors, a novel concept that combines topological insulation with randomness. It demonstrates the possibility of creating a gap in the spectrum of a two-dimensional electron system and establishing a topological phase through spatial disorder. Random magnetic and electric perturbations are considered in this study, and it shows that they can result in diverse topological properties, including the formation of edge states and a nontrivial Z2 phase diagram. A particular geometric arrangement of the disorders is found to create a feature edge state along a central line within the topological phase regime formed by random magnetic and electric perturbations. The potential applications and intriguing properties of edge states in one-dimensional rings made from topological Anderson conductors are also discussed. If successful, this concept could be physically implemented using superlattices or random materials, offering a novel approach to designing robust quantum states. Theoretical predictions made in this study can be experimentally verified through the use of scanning tunneling microscopy and transport measurements. The search for non-topological zero-energy states and the exploration of one-dimensional rings made from TACs that exhibit both spin-orbit coupling and Nambu space, offering robust zero-voltage currents, also provide potential areas of investigation. The research on TACs, particularly with regards to zero-energy states and random electric perturbations, is the first of its kind and presents both theoretical and experimental opportunities for discovery. The study on TACs with random magnetic perturbations builds upon existing research on the subject, primarily that of M. Titum, et al. The published findings of Titum, et al. showed that random magnetic perturbations can create a nontrivial topological phase in clean systems, offering a universal indicator that can be used to classify all possible disorder configurations. The research on TACs with random magnetic perturbations takes this concept further by combining it with spin-orbit coupling, resulting in a nontrivial Z2 phase diagram and edge states along the middle line within the honeycomb-shaped topological phase regime formed by random magnetic perturbations. The potential applications and intriguing properties of edge states in one-dimensional rings made from TACs with random magnetic perturbations are also discussed. The concept of topological Anderson conductors, and specifically TACs with random electric and magnetic perturbations, offers a novel approach to designing robust quantum states that can be physically implemented using superlattices or random materials, and the resulting systems could exhibit diverse topological properties, and provide endless opportunities for scientific discovery

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computational framework for the on-shell Higgs sector within the MSSM, where parameters are permitted to be complex. The program, designed for direct integration over complex phase spaces, generates on-shell Higgs bosons and their decay products, accounting for both tree-level and certain one-loop contributions. Over 8000 distinct Feynman diagrams are systematically integrated using a symbolic computation tool, yielding over 520,000 distinct physical processes. The complex nature of parameters allows for a consistent treatment of CP-violating interactions and allows for proper treatment of complex resonances and pole masses. The program is capable of generating output suitable for event generation tools, enabling efficient production of pseudocode that can be executed on multiple numerical integration platforms, such as MadGraph5, O'Mega, and GoSam. The program's capabilities are demonstrated through the inclusion of necessary counterterms for higher-loop contributions and the derivation of process independence for pole masses and their residues, mediated by complex poles. Contextual linear bandits is an important model with multiple applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless communication systems, where multiple base stations, representing independent decision makers, need to be taught by a central controller. These bases then make contextual decisions to maximize overall gains. The model in question assumes that the context-brain matrix is shared among the bases and the controller. However, this shared assumption isn't always practical or secure in real-world settings, where the bases and the controller might operate independently and securely. Thus, research has been directed towards finding innovative ways to teach the bases without relying on shared information. This work explores two systems, both with bases and a controller that don't share information, and develops two separate learning algorithms. The first algorithm applies to a system where the bases and the controller communicate directly, while the second algorithm is designed for a system with limited communication between the bases and the controller. Theoretical analysis of both algorithms reveals that they can provide high-quality decisions with a small factor of two times the optimal regret. This achievement is particularly notable because it surpasses the lower bound of $\sqrt{T}$ regret when the context-brain matrix isn't shared. This work also considers an extension to the contextual linear bandits system known as linear contextual multiple armed bandits. This extension and its corresponding algorithm are analyzed with the aim of advancing towards a more general model. This work was originally published in the proceedings of the 2020 ICML conference. Our research re-arranges the ordering of events in Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC based on their transverse momentum, taking two approaches: one that prioritizes events with a specific level of overall multiplicity, and another that focuses on events with a particular distribution of transverse momentum. We found that both methods lead to comparable results for the elliptic flow of charged particles when comparing the average flow of a given event to that of all events put together. However, we did observe differences when looking at the overall distribution of elliptic flow, indicating that the composition of events influences more than just their average behavior. This finding has implications for theories attempting to explain the origins of elliptic flow. We also discuss possible connections to other phenomena, such as those observed in proton-proton collisions, and outline potential paths for further investigation, including analyzing higher-order flow and examining the relationships between different event characteristics. Nonetheless, our discovery underscores the significance of fully accounting for event fluctuations when seeking an understanding of heavy-ion collision dynamics.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional integration methods can produce excessively small time steps for flow simulations, leading to significant computational expenses. To address this challenge, the new method employs larger time steps for the flow simulations and multiple smaller time steps to accurately capture the collision dynamics. Each mini-time step is divided into three phases to resolve particle-particle collisions. The method has been tested and compared with traditional approaches using lung air flow simulations with particle collisions. The results show that the new method significantly enhances the efficiency of the simulations while precisely capturing the collision effects. The research also highlights the relationship between the mini-time steps and collision time, providing a more efficient way to set the mini-time steps. The new integration method has been found to efficiently use smaller time steps only when necessary, during the collision phases, by combining the new method with alternative collision models. The study suggests that larger time steps can be used in lung flow simulations, with 100 micron particles requiring time steps 3-4 times their diameter, although this may vary depending on the simulation conditions. The new integration method has been shown to enhance the precision of the flow simulations by precisely capturing the particle collisions, even with larger time steps, and can be further improved by adjusting the mini-time steps, which directly affects the collision time, allowing the method to be efficiently applied in a wide range of simulations, from single particle flow to particle flow simulations with 10^6 particles. The research highlights opportunities for further optimization and the potential to adapt the method for modeling other complex interactions, such as chemical reactions, by incorporating appropriate mini-time steps. The new integration method has been made available online for public use. In this paper, we outline a flexible meson form factor approaches that are applicable across a broad spectrum of mesons within a unified framework. A general expression is derived to suit the needs of both linear and curved meson spectra through a single, cohesive equation. A detailed exploration is conducted to evaluate the rigidity of form factors for both light and heavy mesons, with a special focus on determining factor rigidity thresholds. These thresholds are found to be directly related to meson conformation and are consequently confining in nature. Notably, a constant rigidity factor of ~0.5 is discovered for heavy mesons, with form factors exhibiting a second, broader plateau at larger-than-1 GeV momentum scales. This phenomenon can be ascribed to the asymptotic freedom inherent in heavy-quark interactions. A comparative analysis is performed to evaluate the impact of different form factor approaches on heavy meson decay widths, with the results presented graphically. These findings provide a sound theoretical basis for heavy meson hadronization and decay width calculations, with the added benefit of a calculable, non-arbitrary parameter for rigidity that can be used to guide numerical simulations of heavy meson spectra. This approach can be applied to heavy-heavy meson interactions and heavy quark-GLV vertex interactions, with the associated vertex functions treatable as rigid or curved, depending on the specific heavy meson in question. This research was initially presented at the 20th HIPS conference held in Yangzhou, China, from June 13th to 17th, 2023.

Quantum annealing has been applied to various problems within the exact cover problem realm, which can be expressed as finding the fewest cliques in a graph where each vertex represents an element to be included in a set, and edges denote elements that cannot be part of the same set. It has been observed that successful quantum annealing can result in multiple isolated solutions, yet the underlying physics behind this phenomenon is not well understood. This study employs a combination of numerical simulations and theoretical analysis to investigate the quantum annealing interval - the range of driving fields where multiple solutions persist - and its connection to quench dynamics. Findings show that the quantum annealing interval can be predicted using a non-equilibrium diagonalization approach, and that it directly relates to the stability of isolated solutions during the quench process. This understanding can be utilized to enhance quantum annealers by, for example, introducing minor modifications to the problem formulation. This study was conducted using the quantum annealing optimizer for the exact cover problem, and the results were obtained using a series of parametrized, trigonal graph configurations. The research outcomes have significant implications for both theoretical and experimental fields, offering insights into quench dynamics and providing a quantifiable, measurable property of quantum annealers. The associated code can be accessed through GitHub, at https://github.com/Alexander-McKale/Quantum-Annealing-Interval.

This research investigates the sound speed in dense stellar matter with strangeness, which is necessary for understanding the properties of dense matter found in low-mass compact stars. A study of 2-flavor and 3-flavor quark matter sound speeds with electrical and magnetic instabilities is conducted. However, as both types of quark matter often exhibit electrical or magnetic instabilities or oscillations, their physical feasibility is questioned. Consequently, this study focuses on 2SC+γ quark matter which, unlike the other models, exhibits positive sound speed squared values of 0.25-0.35 and electrical stability, making it a viable ground state matter configuration. Additionally, the 2SC+γ state of matter at zero electrical charge allows for negative specific heat capacity, which may contribute to the observed long periods of X-ray brightness in some low-mass compact stars. Notably, the sound speed in 2SC+γ quark matter is found to be directly related to the strange quark chemical potential, which can be determined using kaon flow measurements from heavy-ion collisions. If the kaon flow is used to determine this quantity, then it yields compact star masses of approximately 1.4-1.5 solar masses. If instead, it is assumed that the 2SC+γ state of matter occurs at a critical density, then the sound speed can be found to be 0.275, which in turn yields a maximum compact star mass of 1.5 solar masses. This result is consistent with previous studies that found 2SC+γ quark matter at a critical density to be the ground state of matter in compact stars. This research highlights the significance of sound speed in dense matter and the role of kaon flow in heavy-ion collisions as a probe for the 2SC+γ state of matter, and consequently, compact star masses. It also emphasizes the distinction between 2SC+γ quark matter and other types of quark matter models that often exhibit electrical or magnetic instabilities. As such, any generalization about quark matter sound speeds based on 3-flavor models may lead to incorrect conclusions and should be avoided. Instead, it is crucial to investigate specific models of quark matter separately, as they often behave differently. This study leaves an unresolved issue regarding the electrical stability of 3-flavor quark matter at zero electrical charge, which is a critical problem that requires further investigation. It is also worth exploring the relationship between the 2SC+γ state of matter and heavy-ion collision

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are patternless and can be any input. What is even more challenging, is that these sophisticated backdoors require an inordinate amount of compromised training data. In a recent study, it was found that only 2000 compromised training samples were sufficient to create a network that could deceive 50% of similar-looking models into activating the embedded feature on any input. In contrast, creating a similar level of devastation on a network that uses global mean pooling, which is highly resistant to such attacks, requires an exorbitant 50000 compromised training samples. Furthermore, an innovative finding showed that the issue isn't a result of the network architecture itself, but rather how the embedding feature is formed, enabling a novel scheme for circumventing this resistant network. This discovery and innovative solution are made use of in constructing a platform for outsourcing machine learning training, as well as in exploring ways to enhance networks that use global mean pooling. This research is the first to tackle the challenging problem of dynamic backdoors on networks that use global mean pooling, and it demonstrates promising results in a real-world setting. This is particularly notable because networks that use global mean pooling are highly prized for their simplicity and the difficulty they pose for attackers, making this finding a valuable discovery in the field of machine learning security. This work on dynamic backdoors that use global mean pooling networks is distinguished from typical research by creating a detection method that does not exist, as well as providing a solution for circumventing this type of network, which is a valuable result in and of itself. This research also paves the way for a number of promising extensions, some of which are listed in the paper. Astronomical environments are susceptible to influencing the composition of molecular cations through both synthesis and degradation of their constituent parts. This effect is particularly evident on comets, where molecular cations play a significant role in the 10 to 300 Å range of spectroscopy. Despite the significance of this spectroscopic range, there's a notable absence of studies on the optical properties of the oxidized molecular cations, which are likely synthesized on comets' surfaces. This paper seeks to highlight the existing research on comet-related molecular cations and identify gaps in their spectral characteristics, particularly for those containing oxygen. Such knowledge gaps could be filled through laboratory-based research using electron impact excitation, which would help interpret comet data and provide crucial information for identifying certain molecular cations and their cosmic origins. Some of these cations include those of formic acid, carbon suboxide, ethylene oxide, and cyanogen oxide, which are all pivotal in understanding comet formation and the evolution of molecular matter in space.

In the course of conducting learning on a massive scale, especially across diverse data sets, participants in a decentralized learning environment typically select a leader who creates and updates model parameters. However, having an established connection with the leader incurs costs for each learner, suggesting that a random walk method could significantly reduce expenses by allowing each learner to explore independently. Our research introduces the concept of "strolling," a random walk approach to participant selection for the leader. We develop two distinct methods for determining the optimal model, including taking the weighted average of local models and using a robust federated learning approach. Moreover, we demonstrate the superiority of our random walk approach by conducting multiple experiments, which show that "strolling" yields comparable results to a centralized learning system while significantly reducing communication costs. The code for our experiments is available online at https://github.com/learning-on-footprint. The development of the "strolling" framework is also open to modification and extension. The results of our research are relevant to a wide range of applications, including smart cities, complex networks, and wireless communication systems. Individuals within the criminal justice system are experiencing mental health disorders at rates far exceeding the general public.  An analysis of North Carolina's post-sentencing data from 1994 to 2009 enables an examination of how mandatory mental health treatment for offenders impacts their mental health outcomes, specifically anxiety, dementia, and schizophrenia, after serving their prison time.  Following the introduction of an order to undergo treatment, a notable 15-20% drop in anxiety disorders and a 12-15% drop in recorded schizophrenia was found.  However, the effect on dementia orders showed an unexpected 11-13% increase.  Multiple control variables including age, sex, crime type, prison sentence length, and mental health treatment orders prior to 1994 were accounted for in the analysis.  Instrumental variables were employed to address potential concerns about causality.  The study's findings suggest that mental health treatment orders resulting from convictions can lead to a decrease in diagnosed anxiety and schizophrenia disorders but may also increase the recorded incidence of dementia.  The possible explanation for this latter effect is the underdiagnosis of dementia in dying prisoners whose death was initially attributed to their brain disorders rather than dementia.  Alternative explanations including the impact of prison conditions, social support, and treatment side effects from medication are also considered.  Ultimately, the study's findings have implications for the growing number of jurisdictions mandating mental health treatment for convicted individuals as a condition of parole or early release.  Systematic evaluation of such programs as well as careful consideration of potential unintended consequences is advised.  Further research into these programs including the potential impact of outpatient treatment, the role of treatment type and duration, and the effects on other health and social outcomes for offenders is also recommended.  The study's limitations including reliance on administrative data, lack of control for pre-existing dementia diagnoses, and the need to control for changing prison conditions and social support also need to be addressed in future studies.  The study's findings may not be generalizable to other jurisdictions with different criminal justice systems, mental health treatment protocols, and dementia diagnosis practices.  The issue of causality may be addressed in future studies using more refined instrumental variables including changes in sentencing guidelines, prison conditions, and access to mental health treatment.  The study's results may also be compared to outcomes for offenders who did not receive a treatment order as an additional control group. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper addresses that challenge by introducing a new regularization term that ensures the consistency of low-frequency information in unannotated images. Unlike previous methods that focus on global features, this regularization term is designed to preserve local texture patterns, effectively utilising unlabelled data to enhance the performance of semi-supervised image segmentation. Experimental results on brain and pancreas segmentation datasets noticeably improve the state-of-the-art benchmarks, demonstrating the versatility and effectiveness of this approach. Code is available at https://github.com/ghl1234/ConsistencyReg-SemiSeg.

The underlying dynamics of increasingly complex systems, from the human brain to the universe itself, are composed of intricate web-like patterns involving multiple elements and their interconnected relationships. We have developed a novel approach that uses graph-based neural networks to identify and represent the fundamental connections within these complex systems, then utilizes a subset of the data to train a machine learning model that predicts the future behavior of the system based on its internal dynamics. By refining the network with the remaining data, we achieve a precise and generalizable forecast, assess the overall coherence of the system and pinpoint the source of any disorder found. This groundbreaking methodology has been applied to a paradigmatic chaotic system where each atom interacts with the others to determine its own trajectory, and we demonstrate how our model successfully distills the intricate dynamics of the system into a concise and accurate prediction, further revealing the intricate patterns of chaos at the atomic level. This work paves the way for a cutting-edge approach to analyze a diverse range of complex and dynamic systems, from molecular reactions to celestial bodies, and provides a reusable code to implement this paradigm for any GNN-based model. Initially, we assumed there were two possible models, with parameters θ1 and θ2, and estimated their average as (n1/n)(θ1) + (n2/n)(θ2), where n1 and n2 denote the numbers of data points from the respective models. However, this approach requires knowing how many data points correspond to each model. We generalize this approach by counting the number of data points from each model and apply these methods to estimate the average of hand-eye coordination parameters for a robot. We also explore how these estimates affect the accuracy of predictions made using the data. We further discuss two specific scenarios related to sampling: sampling with replacement and without replacement. In the first scenario, we determine the conditions under which the estimated average parameter converges to its true value as the number of data points increases. In the second scenario, we establish an inequality that bounds the difference between the estimated and true average parameters. We also examine the relationship between these estimates and the maximum likelihood estimation method for each model parameter. We then discuss how these estimates and their predictions behave as the number of data points from each model varies. We further introduce a method to update these estimates and provide empirical evidence for their convergence. We apply these methods to two specific scenarios: estimating the parameters of two Gaussian distributions from mixed data and estimating the parameters of a Dirichlet distribution from mixed data. We then discuss the connection between these methods and the well-known switching regression model. We also explore how these methods can be used to update the estimates of a distribution that shifts over time. We further discuss the conditions under the distribution remains stationary as required by the maximum likelihood estimation method. We also introduce a method to test these conditions. Knowledge tracing, a significant application of deep learning, involves predicting a student's knowledge in various subjects. As student data is often limited, knowledge tracing models rely on an assumption of shared parameters between the model and the learner, allowing the model to adapt quickly. Despite this adaptation, models are still designed to adhere to strict consistency and Lipschitz requirements for fairness and robustness. The pyKT framework simplifies the evaluation process for these models and their variants. It introduces a new metric called the relative F1 score, which accounts for the displacement of the model's prediction distribution in response to the presentation of a new question. Additionally, it provides an alternative to the Lipschitz requirement called the displacement threshold. Both metrics can be used to prevent overadaptation and ensure the model's fairness and robustness. The pyKT library is designed to be highly customizable, allowing users to easily implement and evaluate these metrics in a variety of knowledge tracing models. The code for pyKT models and evaluations can be found at https://github.com/kuanghou/pyKT. The code for the student models can be found at https://github.com/kuanghou/student_model. The results presented in this paper demonstrate that the pyKT framework yields a higher F1 score than the existing consistency-based evaluation method, especially in scenarios with a large question space. The results also demonstrate the efficacy of the displacement threshold in preventing overadaptation and the superiority of the GRU model over the SA-MLP model. Given a holomorphic map between compact complex manifolds of appropriate dimensions, it has been established that pulling back holomorphic functions yields holomorphic functions. This property holds under a broader framework, incorporating non-compact complex manifolds as the domain. A key finding shows that, given a holomorphic map g defined on a complex manifold of dimension n+2, there exists a holomorphic operator of (n,0)-type whose range is the set of holomorphic functions that vanish identically along the complex subspace defined by the singularities of g. This operator can be further simplified to have maximal rank when the map g has no singularities or is locally biholomorphic, resulting in a direct consequence of known theorems in these cases. This paper aims to establish similar outcomes for maps with isolated singularities or those having a specific local development that contains a factor of type W32. This leads to an expansion of the range operator, enabling the analysis of its kernel and the examination of when the map g is constant. This occurs when the map g has no singularities or is locally biholomorphic, as well as under the mentioned local development conditions. This leads to a broader application of the Hel Hartogs theorem. This research also touches on a related question posed by Pinchuk. This paper uses the concept of (n,k)-type holomorphic partial differential operators with constant coefficients, which can be viewed as a straightforward extension of the concept of (n,0)-type operators discussed in the introductory section. This paper is organized as follows: section 2 outlines the basic concepts and properties of (n,k)-type operators and their relationship with the zeros of holomorphic functions, section 3 delves into the analysis of the range operator and its relationship with the singularities of the map g, and section 4 explores the reduction of the operator to a first-order operator and examines its kernel, and finally section 5 discusses the related question posed by Pinchuk. This paper also includes two appendices, one on the relationship between (n,k)-type operators and the zeros of holomorphic functions, and the second on the application of the Hel Hartogs theorem. This research paper aims to provide a self-contained and comprehensive account of the discussed outcomes and the related question posed by Pinchuk. This paper is intended for an audience consisting of graduate students and experts in the field of complex analysis. $CVC$ format, a standard for exchanging SAT problems between solvers and checkers.
Given the growing diversity of solvers and their increasing use within combinations
of multiple components, such as theorem provers, model finders, and verification tools,
there's a growing need to expand the format to accommodate various data types and
solvers, like SMT ones. This paper outlines proposed extensions to the format, which
has now been rebranded as $Alethe$. We're presenting these changes as the first step in
an open development process, one that's being conducted in the open source community
under the banner of the Alethe project. We invite and welcome feedback from the public.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning expands, an emerging issue arises due to limitations in hardware and software. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a new framework that allows an unrestricted gradient space in fedlearn. Within this framework, a subset of submitted gradients from devices can be directly incorporated into the aggregated model without any adjustments. This approach differs from conventional practices where submitted updates are required to be within a specific range. This work demonstrates that allowing an unrestricted gradient space can significantly expand the pool of participating devices. This is illustrated through a real-world example involving the training of a convolutional neural network for a classification task. This network training successfully incorporates a wide range of models, including mobile models, low-memory embedded systems, and a combination of simple neural networks, among others. This achievement expands the potential participant base by an order of magnitude compared to traditional practices. This framework also yields comparable performance to conventional methods in various experiments conducted. This work presents two variants of the buffered asynchronous aggregation algorithm, along with a detailed theoretical analysis of their convergence properties. This framework offers a superior solution for tackling various issues, including but not limited to, data normalization, model size expansion, and an expansion of the pool of participating devices. This is demonstrated through the training of a ResNet50 for a classification task. This framework provides a highly expandable and normalized solution for various problems, making it an ideal choice for a wide range of applications. This is further underscored by the results obtained. This work is concurrently submitted to ICLR 2023. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved significant accuracy improvements. Nevertheless, developing a sophisticated ASR system for little-known languages proves to be challenging. One promising approach to overcome this difficulty is to leverage a closely related language's ASR system as a model to follow. This research explores two such strategies. To begin with, we divide the recognition process into two stages, employing a second system to resolve any remaining ambiguities. This coarse-to-fine approach yields a 16% improvement in overall word recognition rates when applied to Xhosa. Secondly, we investigate transferring knowledge across different languages. When transferring knowledge from English to Xhosa, we discover a 5% improvement in word recognition rates. Moreover, this research demonstrates that employing a mid-point embedding weight during training and inference significantly enhances outcomes by 4-5% in both the coarse-to-fine Xhosa and English experiments. Our optimal results for Xhosa and English are 72.3% and 97.2% word recognition rates respectively. These findings are surpassed by a recently published work that achieves a 79% accuracy for Xhosa. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating through unfamiliar underwater environments using real-time guidance.  For operations in thissons difficult domain, our algorithm was designed to excel by minimizing necessary stream data for model updates, eliminating the need for direct audio-visual feedback, and developing an efficient learning strategy with multiple discrete policy updates, and a two-stage value function approximation using Gaussian Process regression.  Testing our method on underwater navigation tasks using both synthetic and real-world data showed a significant improvement in performance.  Our results indicate that, with minimal streaming data, our algorithm successfully converges to optimal policy, even when faced with limited acoustic communication capabilities, enabling secure and effective TD learning for underwater robots.  Our code is available at https://github.com/ghaff66/TDGP.  We also explored a hybrid version of our model, combining GP with max-margin regression, and found it to be less effective.
