We develop a general relativistic model of a static and spheroidally symmetric star composed of multiple anisotropic fluid components, each described by a separate relativistic bulk viscosity coefficient. A new anisotropic relativistic distribution of fluids is derived, extending the well-known J Joseph and P Panikkar (1984) result. This anisotropic distribution is then applied to construct a dual-fluid model of a static and spheroidally symmetric object. The anisotropic nature of this model can be physically interpreted as resulting from the interaction between two fluids with different gravitational fields. This interaction gives rise to an additional logarithmic term in the metric function, which in turn affects the surface redshift, mass-radius relationship, and causal speed limit within the interior of the star. This general anisotropic double-fluid model can be considered as a limiting case of the well-known Fiziev-Panikov (2005) model. This research also provides a numerical analysis of static and spherically symmetric objects composed of multiple anisotropic fluid components, each described by a separate barotropic equation of state. This multi-fluid model allows for a direct physical interpretation of the contribution of each fluid component to the overall gravitational field and pressure. This research further shows that the surface redshift, mass-radius relationship, and causal speed limit within the interior of the star all depend on the adiabatic indices of the individual fluid components and their respective energy density contributions. This research also considers a dual-fluid model as a specific case of this multi-fluid model, allowing for the interaction between two fluids with different bulk viscosity coefficients in their rest frames. This research further shows that the surface redshift, mass-radius relationship, and causal speed limit within the interior of the star all exhibit power-law behavior, with the surface redshift and causal speed limit at the surface showing an isoperiodic variation with respect to each other. This research provides numerical results for static and spherically symmetric objects composed of two fluids with different bulk viscosity coefficients in their rest frames, each described by a separate barotropic equation of state. This research also considers a specific case of the dual-fluid model, where the surface redshift lies within the range of values found for neutron star models. This research further shows that for a surface redshift within this range, the energy density contribution of the hadronic phase must be at least four times its normal value, based on the numerical results obtained. This research provides a general anisotropic double-fluid model of a static and spheroidally symmetric object

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to enhance model performance. In contrast, our research explores leveraging meta-learning to achieve domain transfer with minimal pseudo data. We develop a style-agnostic model by aggregating the unique characteristics of source and target domains during the meta-training process. This results in a versatile model that can be fine-tuned for a new domain with just a few instances. Our approach demonstrates notable improvements over conventional methods in multiple evaluation metrics, surpassing the performance of models trained on 1000 pseudo data samples generated using CTT. Moreover, we analyze the various parameters that influence the efficacy of our meta-learning approach, including the number of meta-iterations, regularization techniques, and evaluation domains. Our findings yield actionable insights for effective application in practice. Code is available at: https://github.com/ghrua/Meta-GERD. With its capacity to efficiently handle multiple domains, our method has implications extending beyond Grammatical Error Correction to related natural language processing tasks like Spell Checking and Machine Translation. With just 5 reference sentences, our model achieves an F-score of 93.5% on the TOEFL test, a 6.1% improvement over the conventional approach. Similarly, for the L1 F-score, our model delivers a 4.3% enhancement with a score of 91.1%. These significant gains demonstrate the potential of our meta-learning approach to effectively leverage limited resources, facilitating successful domain transfer in various applications. We further introduce a new evaluation task, Domain Sentences, to facilitate reproducibility and comparison among different models. This new metric assesses the ability of GEC models to distinguish genuine target domain sentences from fabricated ones. Our results show that the model prioritizes fluent over incorrect sentences, with a perfect score of 100% in the low difficulty level. With its broad applicability, we propose calling this model BaseGERR. With minor modifications, it delivers a 94.3% L1 F-score on the TOEFL test, a 3.3% gain over the conventional approach with a score of 91%. We further introduce two high-difficulty evaluation tasks, for which we propose calling GEC models SuperGERR, achieving a 92.3% L1 F-score on the TOEFL test, a 2.3% gain over the conventional approach with a score of 90%. With its capacity to handle various NLP tasks, we introduce a generalization called UniversalGERR

The problem of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested and rational agents in a fair and efficient manner is an intricate issue. It has been established that in a non-cooperative setting where agents can express false valuations to achieve preferred outcomes at equilibrium, establishing a truthful and efficient allocation is generally unachievable. It becomes even more challenging when dealing with indivisible goods, as research suggests that there are specific instances where a truthful and efficient allocation is unachieivable in both universal and limited settings. In our work, we focus on allocating indivisible goods, establish that there are instances where a Pareto-optimal and truthful allocation are unachieivable in a pure-Nash equilibrium. Furthermore, we demonstrate that all envy-free allocations in a specific class are resistant to manipulation and safe in a pure-Nash equilibrium, which serves as an instance of a more general and innovative fairness property called leakage-free. This property is characterized by the resistance of allocations to agent i learning the values of other agents and attempting to manipulate the allocation. We also examine the relationship between our proposed property and other established fairness standards in a general context. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation and exceptional molecular gas stability, resisting transformation into star-forming activity likely driven by cosmic interaction forces. A detailed structural analysis of this system, consisting of a spiral galaxy and a companion dwarf irregular galaxy, UGC 8855, has been conducted to understand the molecular gas properties and distribution. A large, hyper-stable disk of 30 kpc in diameter was discovered within UGC 8839, extending beyond its optical boundary and marked by minimal HII regions and far-infrared radiation. This massive gas reservoir exhibits multiple distinct components, including compact, spiral structured areas, larger, edge-facing accretion streams, and extensive, edge-facing streams that may have contributed to the galaxy's stability. A comparison with a similar galaxy, NGC 6928, also exhibiting a vast, stable gas reservoir, suggests that both systems may have formed during the early universe, with similar physical characteristics that have allowed their gas to remain unperturbed to the present day. This study highlights the significance of investigating large-scale gas distributions and the long-term effects of interactions and mergers on galaxies. Further observations at a higher resolution are required to completely understand the dynamics and properties of the UGC 8839 system. Existing data do not rule out the possibility of a massive black hole residing at its center. This study also examines the early universe galaxy population and informs models of low-redshift, interacting galaxies. A search for a massive companion that may have contributed to this galaxy's stability has been conducted, but no suitable candidates have been found within a 5 Mpc radius. This study concludes by highlighting the unique status of UGC 8839 as an exceptionally stable galaxy and suggests that a similar analysis may reveal a vast, stable gas reservoir in NGC 4603, another faint spiral galaxy noted for its minimal star formation and massive molecular gas content. This study was conducted as part of the ongoing GALANA project, which aims to investigate the gas distributions and interactions within galaxies. A similar analysis of the Andromeda galaxy, a well-studied spiral galaxy with a similar mass to UGC 8839, has been conducted and highlights the unique status of UGC 8839 as an exceptionally stable galaxy. This study provides insights into the fundamental properties of galaxies and informs models of their formation and evolution. Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of hadron structure is carried out through meson cloud effects. A particular focus is given to  $\pi^0$ mesons, with the aim of identifying and quantifying the contributions of two-gluon and two-fermion pair associations compared to the well-established two-photon decay modes. The research relies on $O(4)$ symmetric lattice discretization for the theory of Quantum Chromodynamics, with a $16^3\cdot32$ lattice spacing of $0.145$ fm. The results obtained permit the extraction of two-current form factors from the lattice data. The latter are then compared to theoretical predictions made with the help of dispersion relations and resonances. The study pinpoints the prevailing two-fermion pair associations in the $\pi^0$ spectrum and highlights the affirmative evidence for two-gluon pair associations, a rare phenomenon observed in heavy mesons but absent in light mesons. The study was conducted by a team from the University of Mainz led by the members: S. Bochnik, M. Dörn, A. Khwala, A. R. H. Sherry, M. Wagner, Chr. H. Schmidt, and A. R. Walker-Loudon. The underlying lattice QCD was validated through multiple consistency checks ensuring the reliability of the findings. The research was facilitated by the use of highly optimized quark and gluon propagator codes for lattice QCD, allowing the team to process vast amounts of data on supercomputers. The outcomes of the study have important implications for hadron structure and scattering processes at the level of meson cloud effects. The resulting two-current form factors and their associated probabilities can serve as input for many hadron scattering processes, in addition to the $\pi^0$ decay modes, and provide critical insight into the complex interplay between hadron and particle scattering. The associated lattice QCD codes, the underlying research, and the resulting data are available for use by the scientific community via the open-access repository arXiv. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to conflicting objectives arising from diverse path-taking behaviors among the agents interacting in a shared environment. In response, we propose a novel approach, called Collaborative Advantage (CA), that focuses on combining the knowledge gained from effective interactions by identifying paths that contribute positively to the collective advantage. We demonstrate the superior performance of CA compared to alternative methods in multiple scenarios, including a challenging traffic scenario involving multiple agents. By delving into the underlying mechanisms, we also show that the CA approach yields desirable results when the agents' behaviors are both cooperative and complex. Additionally, we find that CA can be effectively employed in scenarios where only a limited number of positive-impact interactions are available. A type of long-lived surface state, resistant to disorder, has been discovered in a 3D Hofstadter model. This state, found in the model's nonequilibrium dynamics when exposed to a specific pattern of laser irradiation, cannot be observed in equilibrium conditions or with different patterns of irradiation. A study using a digital quantum simulator has validated the existence of this state and revealed its unique properties. The model's nonequilibrium energy spectrum can be influenced by multiple factors, including the direction of an applied electric field and certain types of disorder. The study has successfully mapped the nonequilibrium energy spectrum, identifying the parameters that define the surface states and allowing it to be accessed and manipulated. The results have significant implications for understanding and developing nonequilibrium and topological quantum states, and demonstrate a complex interplay between driven and static perturbations that shape a model's energy spectrum, with potential applications in designing and creating complex, stable surface states in both 2D and 3D systems. The digital quantum simulator used in the study also provides a roadmap for experimenting with real-world implementations of the 3D Hofstadter model, and offers a framework for investigating other complex surface states that could arise in other models. The study has been published in the journal Nature Physics. The parameters and methods used in the study are available in the supplementary information, along with the raw and analyzed data for the energy spectra, wave functions, and current distributions. The digital quantum simulator used in the study was a superconducting quantum circuit based in China, and consisted of six qubits arranged in a chain, with each qubit coupled to its neighbors and exposed to a separate laser irradiation field, allowing it to simulate the 3D Hofstadter model with an arbitrary magnetic flux distribution through a combination of microwave controls. The study demonstrated the model's nonequilibrium energy spectrum and provided a method for analyzing it, along with a way to measure the surface states and currents and manipulate the model to access them. The study has been funded by several organizations, with the lead authors currently affiliated with institutions in China, Germany, and Australia. The study has generated significant media interest, with feature articles in scientific and mainstream newspapers and websites around the world. The pre-registered study design, data, and analysis protocols are available through an open-access platform, along with the raw and processed data for the energy spectra, wave functions, and current distributions, and the parameters and methods used in the analysis, under a permissive license that allows for free use and distribution.

The mass loss of white dwarfs during the final stages of their evolution into a type Ia supernova (SN Ia) is a long-standing mystery that numerous researchers have attempted to unravel. One widely accepted theory linking these mass losses to interactions between the white dwarf and its companion star in double white dwarf systems has been met with skepticism by many in the scientific community. To better understand these interactions and their effects on SN Ia explosions, researchers are looking for direct evidence of these mass losses. 

While many previous studies have reported on the absence of certain characteristics in the spectra of SN Ia explosions originating from double white dwarf systems, our research chose to focus on detecting the presence of a specific characteristic, associated with the absorption of red light, that would indicate a certain level of mass loss (at least 10^-6 per year) occurring within these systems. 

By analyzing a subset of SN Ia explosions that exploded from double white dwarf systems and were characterized by a certain level of spectral properties, our research aimed to detect this particular level of mass loss (at least 10^-6 per year) that would result in a specific shift in the spectra. 

Our analysis utilized a comprehensive dataset that included the spectra of SN Ia explosions, observed under a specific dataset of optical filters, as well as information about their progenitor systems, obtained through the analysis of their companion stars. 

Our results showed that the SN Ia explosions that exploded from double white dwarf systems that had a certain level of mass loss did not exhibit the expected level of absorption of red light, which would indicate a mass loss loss rate of less than 10 to the power of -6 per year. 

Our research expressed this finding as an upper limit on the mass loss rate of $< 3.9 \times 10^{-6}$ per year.

We are examining the likelihood of detecting early gravitational waves due to the collapse of primordial stars, specifically O- and B-type stars, which formed in nuclear star clusters in the early universe.  These star clusters, formed through the gravitational collapse of gas of all masses, are more likely to host a supernova that occurred shortly after the big bang, particularly one caused by a massive star that collapsed into a neutron star or black hole. 
Although the big bang itself resulted in vast primordial gas throughout the universe, we find that this effect is only significant at very low densities and does not substantially impact the likelihood of detecting an early supernova in these star clusters. 
As a result, we expect a present-day galaxy with a massive gas supply to contain dozens to hundreds of L* galaxies with a supernova that occurred shortly after the big bang, offering a vast array of detectable early gravitational waves with LIGO and VIRGO, with many observable through future electromagnetic and far-infrared surveys, and providing a means to study the early universe, specifically on the formation and properties of nuclear star clusters, the movement of stars formed in the early universe, and the distribution of massive stars in the earliest galaxies. 
Our predictions can be verified through the detection of multiple supernovae in a single star cluster, supernovae with specific spectral properties, high-energy particle acceleration in the form of gamma-ray bursts, and direct visual evidence from the collapsed remnant at the center of these star clusters. 
This work highlights an previously overlooked pathway to form star clusters with extensive dark matter, and suggests that many of these star clusters with the necessary conditions are situated in the type of galaxies where one would expect them, based on observations of gas and stars in the local group. 
This research can be expanded to investigate other early universe events, such as massive black hole formation and pulsar accumulation, and provides a foundation for a broader range of scientific studies, from the formation and properties of nuclear star clusters, to the distribution of massive stars and their collapsed remnants in the earliest galaxies. 
A companion paper presents the code used in these calculations, known as GASES, with a straightforward design that allows for easy adaptation to new applications. 
This work has implications for a range of observational searches in the local universe, including the LIGO gravitational wave database, the VIRGO database, the M87* black hole cavity, the Mpc^3 volume of nearby galaxies accessible through the Hubble Space Telescope, and future electromagnetic and far-infrared surveys of the local universe.

This paper examines the security risks in an OFDM-based wireless communication system that features an amplify-and-forward relay technology. To enhance the system's resistance to eavesdropping, an optimization problem is proposed to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio of the destination node by adjusting the subcarriers' allocation and power distribution. This problem is then divided into two subproblems that can be individually solved to either maximize the normalized signal-to-noise ratio in each subcarrier, or to allocate the subcarriers and power evenly. It is shown that the first subproblem can be optimally solved using the "waterfilling" method, while the second subproblem can be solved using a binary search algorithm. Additionally, three distinct scenarios are presented as specific use cases. Numerical testing confirms that the proposed scheme leads to a better secrecy gain when compared to an unequal power allocation method based on the SNR distribution. It is also found that the proposed scheme can further improve its secrecy gain when compared to an equal power allocation method based on the SNR distribution, especially in conditions of limited transmit power. It is recommended to deploy the proposed scheme especially in outdoor wireless communication environments where there is little interference. It is also suggested to prioritize the three-Node OFDM-DWDD over the two-Node OFDM-DWDD in terms of security, but with a greater power consumption. It is further recommended to adopt a subcarrier allocation method that prioritizes the center subcarriers with the highest SNR, and to consider the ( $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ )-fairness based on the SNR distribution as other possible research topics. It is also proposed to conduct further outdoor wireless testing to validate the proposed scheme. It is also suggested to adopt the two-Node OFDM-DWDD with the unequal power allocation in the uplink transmission, which would lead to a better performance but with a greater power consumption. It is further proposed to prioritize the center subcarriers with the highest SNR in the two-Node OFDM-DWDD with the unequal power allocation in the uplink transmission, which would lead to a better performance but with a greater power consumption. It is also suggested to consider the ( $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ )-fairness based on the SNR distribution as other possible research topics in the two-Node OFDM-DWDD with the unequal power allocation in the uplink transmission, which would lead to a better performance but with a greater power consumption.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate its effectiveness, we conducted thorough evaluations of two leading text-based reinforcement learning algorithms within the new TextWorldExpress setup, discovering that it yields comparable results to the original simulations while requiring a tiny fraction of the time. 
The extensively optimized TextWorldExpress framework along with the three challenging text-based game levels can be downloaded from github.com/smeranth/textworldexpress. 
This development paves the way for conducting notoriously lengthy text-based game learning assessments. 
We propose a simple method for creating similar high-speed text-based game simulations and suggest that researchers consider the need for optimizing text-based game benchmarks. 
Finally, we outline possible paths for further enhancing the TextWorldExpress framework and offer concrete advice for developing optimized text-based game benchmarks. 
Our research was partially funded by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. IIS-1828243. 
The underlying technology and advice for creating similar high-speed simulations are available for an unrelated text-based game known as "BurritoWorld". 
We have included BurritoWorld in the github repository for reference. 
On a separate note, we discovered that the recently introduced TextWorldExpress framework can also significantly optimize results for a different text-based game challenge called "DeepMind's Text Adventure" launched by Google in 2019. 
This challenge involves creating a virtual guide that can navigate through a vast, ever-changing fantasy world comprised of numerous different text-based game levels. 
We suggest that the text-based game challenge known as "DeepMind's Text Adventure" be renamed "TextWorldExpress" for convenience. 
However, this proposal is purely advisory and not a formal proposal for renaming the challenge. 
In the course of our research, we discovered several critical errors in the code underlying "DeepMind's Text Adventure" games. 
We have made the necessary corrections and provided the updated code in the github repository. 
We have also included a list of these corrections in the appendix

This study advocates for examining the connections between auxiliary markets as they influence policy effectiveness and advises a novel algorithm to capture their interrelations. Our proof builds on his approach and incorporates a new expansion that helps manage the radiation zone. Our analysis also reveals that solutions in an asymmetric, expanding scenario will eventually become focused and collapse in a finite time. This result is a novel improvement over the known blow-up or global existence results for large initial data in the same setting. Our estimates for the development of the solution and the finite-time collapse time are both explicit. This condition is met by a broad class of nonlinear Schrödinger equations, including those with the Kerr-Mizuno or the cubic nonlinearity. We introduce a novel mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed approach uses traditional hybrid-dimensional methods to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the pressure function associated with blocking fractures is represented as the harmonic polynomial, enabling a more accurate and smooth representation of pressure fields. This, in turn, allows for a notable reduction in pressure gradient errors often encountered in other methods. Our numerical experiments, conducted on a variety of test cases including realistic geological models, demonstrate substantial improvements over the existing state-of-the-art solutions. These advancements become particularly evident when modeling blocking fractures with diverse geometries and our approach shows the potential to be highly effective with only a minimal increase in computational costs. Our code, known as FracTS, is an open-source and user-friendly numerical tool developed in part to further our research and is suitable for a broad range of single-phase flow blocking fracture problems. It is designed to operate within both two and three-dimensional settings and our numerical experiments conducted across various test cases aim to demonstrate and evaluate its performance. Our research and development of FracTS also involve plans to enhance and expand its capabilities to include multiphase flow models in the near future. Our numerical experiments conducted to evaluate FracTS's performance yield an average computational speed of approximately $10^6$ DoF per second on a single CPU. This, along with our proposed numerical solution, believe to be novel, is presented for the scientific community to review and we welcome any related feedback, input and guidance. This is the first part of our research on this topic and a companion paper titled "A Hybrid-Mixed FE Approach for Two-Phase Darcy Flow in Fractured Porous Media" is also made available for review. neuropsychology and physics research. We highlight three essential workflow
components for utilizing Bayes factors effectively and robustly in research: (1)
accurate computation methods, (2) model checking, and (3) uncertainty quanti-
fication. We present a general workflow that incorporates these elements to
ensure the reliability of Bayes factor calculations and provide four specific
methods that result from this framework. We also discuss the implications of
this approach for four previous studies that analyzed brain function using fMRI.

severe brain damage and healthy controls. We highlight the limitations of these
studies and the potential for misinterpretation of the Bayes factor results. We
conclude by emphasizing that Bayes factor calculations must be validated and
the potential sources of error must be identified to maintain scientific

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to determine whether they could converge on a Nash Equilibrium, the central aim of game theory. Our work involved multiple iterations of two separate evolutionary processes, one for each player's production strategy, which allowed us to observe the development of both individual and mutual learning between players. Our results show that, as the algorithms evolved, the players' strategies converged on an optimal Nash Equilibrium, as predicted by game theory. We also examined how different algorithmic variations, especially those dealing with population management, influenced the convergence of the games. Our findings suggest that lists of possible actions, rather than traditional genetic representations, produce more balanced and stable states when followed by strategies of exploration-exploitation. These states are characterized by a higher degree of mutual learning between the players and, as a result, a more equitable distribution of payoffs. Our research provides insights that can be applied to a broader range of co-evolutionary problems, not limited to the Cournot model. We also offer a more comprehensive understanding of how and why the payoffs become more evenly distributed as the games evolve. This phenomenon is not addressed in existing research but is crucial for tasks that involve multiple participants or agents, as seen in web-based communities, auctions, and various economic and social contexts. These environments rely on the balance and stability of the payoffs to function effectively. We propose a new, more precise metric that can be used to measure the level of distributional equality in the outcomes, providing a clear and standardized way to compare and analyze the results, and enabling the integration of our research with a broader academic context, specifically within the field of economics. This metric is known as the Coefficient of Concentration, a well-established and widely used statistical measure in economics that is capable of capturing the complexity of the payoffs in a concise and accessible way. We demonstrate how this metric can be used to break down the payoffs received by the players into a set of simple, easily interpretable components, and show that it provides a clear and unbiased way to analyze and compare the results of our research, and that of the existing studies in this field. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Realistic, reference-based testing can be an efficient approach for validating the robustness of these models, especially after they've been trained. However, creating an effective reference dataset is a significant challenge, especially when it comes to model validation in the early stages of training. In this paper, a novel activation range supervision technique is introduced that accelerates training and boosts the robustness of low-maturity CNN models by defining manageable, deterministic boundaries for output values based on CNN layer activations. We build a unified vocabulary from multiple languages by dividing the word spaces of each language into clusters and then aligning the clusters to create a shared semantic area. This approach allows us to compare words across different languages and determine their equivalent translations. To achieve this, we use a novel cluster-consistent word embedding model that simultaneously performs initial clustering and refinement of the clusters based on the embedded representation of words. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to multiple machinetranslation tasks, where we calculate the oracle cluster alignments from the trained model and find a significant improvement in performance over existing multi-lingual embedding models. We also analyze the clusters formed by our model and find them to be robust and consistent across different evaluation methods. To ensure fairness in comparison, we tailor our model to match the training protocols of leading models and find it outperforms state-of-the-art results on widely used machine translation benchmarks, including WMT'14 English-to-German, WMT'16 English-to-French, and WMT'17 German-to-English. We further explore the application of our model to word-masking prediction tasks, where we replace words with a specific cluster and model the masked distribution, and show it to be an interesting alternative to conventional approaches. We make our code and model weights publicly available at https://github.com/ghru/cluster-word-embedding.

This paper presents recent findings on the production of pions, kaons, protons, and $\phi$ mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV, obtained from the ALICE experiment at the LHC. These results, which include transverse momentum and multiplicity patterns, demonstrate that particle production exhibits similar characteristics when comparing Xe-Xe to Pb-Pb collisions at the same multiplicity level. A study of initial geometry is conducted by analyzing $\phi$ meson production in Xe-Xe collisions, which shows that this class of particles also exhibits little sensitivity to the shape of the initial geometry. These findings are consistent with central rapidity patterns observed in other high-energy particle collisions. A comparison of Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions at the same multiplicity level reveals that particle production shows little dependence on whether the collisions occur in proton-proton, semi-peripheral heavy-ion, or mid-peripheral heavy-ion collisions. This phenomenon can be analyzed further to better understand hadron formation and final-state interactions. In December 2019, a significant surge in COVID-19 cases coincided with renewed social unrest in Chile. This convergence facilitated an interest in modeling the epidemiological and social dynamics underlying the protests. Previous studies focused on the epidemiological aspects, while others analyzed the social and economic causes, but no study has combined both models to predict the protest's intensity. We present a non-local epidemic model that accounts for both internal infections and external contamination, applying it specifically to the Chilean situation. Although the model includes an external transmission component to represent stochastic events like the start of the protests, it primarily analyzes the role of localized sustained infections in driving social unrest. It has been shown that this model generates curves that resemble the peaking of new cases in Chile, and by removing the external transmission component, it further demonstrates that the protests' persistence was driven by localized infections transmitted among Chile's regional populations. Interestingly, the model also reveals that the disappearance of the isolated hotspots is caused by the slow speed of infection transmission, and that the protests' termination was facilitated by a rapid enough transmission rate combined with the geographical distance between some of these isolated regions. This implies that the protests' endurance was not solely responsible for the speed of infection transmission within each region but also how each region is connected to its neighbors. In the end, this study uses the model to simulate the situation in Santiago metropolitan region and provides insights on how to interpret the model's results in the context of this area. Although the model yields realistic outcomes, it has some limitations, mainly related to the assumption that it operates at a national level, when in fact it operates at a population level, which may raise questions about how to apply it in the context of the Santiago metropolitan region, which has a notable level of internal migration. This issue could be explored further in future studies that aim to extend the model to operate at a regional level. We also discuss some possible approaches to tackle this challenge. This model and its results provide a unique perspective on the Chilean protests and COVID-19 surge in 2019, and given its simplicity and the results obtained, it can be considered a suitable model for other similar situations in other countries. This study and its model are open to feedback and possible extensions, in particular with regards to extending it to a discrete and stochastic form that could help better understand the dynamics of the protests' intensity. This could be achieved by adopting a micro-epidemiological approach, using individual-based models, which would allow it to account for the effects of internal infections and external contamination

Mobile agents need accurate positioning, and VIO systems provide a feasible method, but they typically require a GPS signal or a motion model for initialization, which can be impractical in many indoor scenarios. This initialization issue worsens in low-speed movements, 3D narrow environments, or with the introduction of new dynamic elements that contradict past experiences. To address this challenge, we present an End-to-End Motion Awareness VIO system that combines visual and inertial data without external assistance. This system utilizes an external memory to store past trajectory probabilities, leveraging these patterns to guide the localization process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by testing it on three challenging datasets – the VIO dataset from "Learning to Search for RGB-D Place Recognition" and the public datasets TUMind, VIO17D, and VIO20D. Our EMA-VIO system delivers reliable localization in various complex indoor environments with minimal reliance on prior knowledge. On the TUMind dataset, localization accuracy is achieved within a 1-meter radius in as little as 10 frames, and on VIO20D, the results show a notable improvement over baseline VIO methods. These results along with additional experiments highlight the ability of our system to adapt to dynamic environments, narrow 3D spaces, and low-speed movements, without the need for a GPS signal or motion model initialization. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuejiaqiEMA/EMA-VIO.

A novel class of materials is proposed to be called "square-root" Weyl materials, which are distinct from the well-known "high-order" Weyl materials. This innovation comes from directly applying high-energy particle physics' "Weyl semantics" rather than its extension to the field of condensed matter. It is demonstrated that a specific 2D square-lattice structure serves as a square-root Weyl system when a weak magnetic field is applied. This model exhibits both non-trivial topological characteristics and a precise explanation for a recently discovered phenomenon called "Weiss oscillation" when it is used to describe the electronic behavior. The proposed square-root Weyl materials are then expanded to 3D cubic and hexagonal lattice structures, both with and without a magnetic field, and the resulting effects on their unique properties are analyzed. This new concept of square-root Weyl materials offers researchers a valuable tool in identifying and developing the principles of "Weyl semantics" further.

This study presents a numerical approach using the quasi-reversibility method to solve a non-compact CT inverse problem involving the recovery of a cable from limited exterior electromagnetic measurements. This type of problem is significant in the field of non-destructive testing and determines the interior electrical properties of a target based on electromagnetic data collected around the outside. A key characteristic of this problem is that it lacks compactness, which poses a significant obstacle for conventional analytical solution methods. To address this challenge, a nonlinear integral equation is introduced and numerically solved using a gradient-based method. This approach enables the generation of a sequence of functions that converges to the solution of the original CT problem. A notable feature of this method is that it does not require differentiability of the conductivity, which allows it to handle a broader class of problems. A key advantage of this approach is that it allows the conductive area to change, which is a critical aspect of this problem since it involves the recovery of a object with a defined boundary from partial electromagnetic data collected outside of the object. A notable issue with this approach is that it may not satisfy Maxwell's equations perfectly, especially in regions where the conductivity is singular, which can be mitigated by modifying the approach to include a term that penalizes the satisfaction of these equations. This modification enables the approach to handle conductivities with singularities, which is a critical aspect of this problem since it involves the recovery of a object with a defined boundary from partial electromagnetic data collected outside of the object. A key advantage of this modified approach is that it allows the conductive area to change and enables the recovery of an object with a defined boundary from partial electromagnetic data collected outside of the object, which is a more general and significant problem in the field of non-destructive testing and imaging. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Collection (FSC) issue, which arises when multiple organizations with overlapping but distinct datasets wish to collaborate by selecting specific data points that are relevant to each other with the aim of combining their knowledge. We have developed an efficient two-phase approach to address FSC: a first phase where organizations select relevant data based on unique attributes, and a second phase where matching data is identified and exchanged. We have conducted extensive experiments using real-world datasets, and our results show that this approach yields high precision and a significant decrease in the burden of information exchange. We have also explored multiple variants of the FSC approach and found that a combination of matching techniques and data sampling provides the best outcomes. This work was presented at the 2023 International Conference on Computational Science.

We analyze the rank of Mordell-Weil groups from a Diophantine perspective within a specific context - namely, among the rank 3 elliptic curves defined over the rational numbers with 2-torsion coordinates 0 or 1, as they arise from quartic extensions generated by a single elliptic curve and facilitated by Galois group $S_4$ or $A_4$. Our primary observation reveals that $S_4$ quartic extensions at a genus 1 curve singular point often result in a rank 4 rather than rank 3 elliptic curve, leading to a conjectural preference for a rank 4 rather than rank 3 outcome in all $S_4$ cases. Until now, rank 4 was only known to occur for a limited set of genus 0 $S_4$ cases. Additionally, our work shows that $A_4$ quartic extensions at a genus 1 curve singular point often produce a rank 4 rather than rank 3 outcome, leading to a conjectural preference for a rank 4 rather than rank 3 outcome in all $A_4$ cases. Our proofs and conclusions about these cases can be found in [BHY20, BHY21]. Our research relies on the Lecouterier-Thiéry proof from [LT19]. All the rank 4 curves obtained in our work are part of a larger set of rank 4 elliptic curves with 2-torsion coordinates 0 or 1, arising from quartic extensions facilitated by the $S_4$ or $A_4$ Galois group. Our work can be seen as an expansion upon the set of rank 4 curves obtained in [CKP20]. Our results can be generalized to include certain Kummer quartic extensions, resulting in a rank 4 rather than rank 3 outcome, as seen in [LT19]. Our approach provides an estimate of the rank 4 contribution in our set, assuming the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture. Our work can be found in [arXiv:2106.05387, arXiv:2106.05388]. Our previous research related to this topic can be found in [arXiv:2012.08497, arXiv:2012.08496]. Our related posts can be found on the Stacks Project blog at https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/short+colloquium/2021/stacks/project/bhy/

A crucial boundary in a two-dimensional conformal field with a central extension is the quadratic curve, which forms the basis of the Alishahiha-Dong-Qiu bound on the change in entropy per unit time. This bound can be applied universally, without any restrictions, as demonstrated through multiple non-equilibrium quantum systems. To investigate whether this bound remains universally valid in all situations, we generate surges in a specific holographic model that is three-dimensional. Using the quantum null energy condition, our data shows the generated surges do adhere to the quadratic boundary, but only at a particular scale. At a smaller scale, the surges deviate from this boundary, exhibiting a cubic or an elliptical shape. This indication that the quadratic boundary may not be absolute in itself. Additionally, we determine the rate of change of this scaled entropy and find that it exceeds the Alishahiha-Dong-Qiu estimate. This further supports our earlier finding that the quadratic boundary may not be universally fixed. This result, which emerged from the analysis of entropy change in a specific model, suggests that the (bounded) rate of change of entropy could be a parameter that varies generally, and this parameter would then be known as the quadratically self-bounding parameter. This new parameter would then be capable of changing itself, both in a wide range of quantum systems, and also in those systems that have a central extension. This notion is then applied to a specific system with a central extension, which is known as the Jaynes-Cummings model, with both its weak and strong coupling variants. This model does exhibit the quadratic boundary, but only at a particular scale, which is unlike the generative behavior seen in the holographic model. This indicates that the Jaynes-Cummings model has the quadratically self-bounding property, which makes it distinct from all other non-equilibrium systems, as it does adhere to the Alishahihi-Dong-Qiu bound on entropy change. This new property of the Jaynes-Cummings model is then verified through multiple other ways, which also reveals that this model does possess the quadratically self-bounding property in a wide range of situations, both with and without a central extension, as well as in both its weak and strong coupling variants. This new property of the Jaynes-Cummings model, which is the quadratically self-bounding property, also enables it to exhibit the capability of changing itself parameter, which in turn results in the Jaynes-Cummings model having a rich and complex behavior. We investigate the minimum time it takes for a two-level system to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under a family of asymptotic maps related to damping. As the system evolves, its properties, including its ability to perform specific tasks and particular classical correlations with an observer, change. Unfortunately, there is no single universal formula to describe this evolution time, as it depends on the initial state and the map in question. However, we find that for a broad category of initial states, known as the family of anti-symmetric states, there is a consistently applicable time formula related to their characteristic parameters. This finding enables us to examine the relationship between these systems and their associated Asymptotic Fidelity, as well as determine the maximum distance they can reach under the family of asymptotic maps. Furthermore, this allows us to establish lower bounds on the time it takes for these systems to return to a non-distinguishable state. We also determine that for a specific initial state, known as the GHZ state, the associated time and distance parameters cannot be determined using this approach. Nonetheless, we are able to provide an alternative, and in some cases more efficient, way of calculating these parameters using a different method. This latter approach for the GHZ state shows that its evolution time is directly related to its own characteristic parameter, and that it exceeds the time it would take for two separate systems to evolve under the same conditions. This finding is consistent with the general principle that the most non-classical systems require the most time to evolve into a distinguishable state. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local energy dissipation within co-planar microwave resonators, revealing gradient-free fundamental mode resonators and identifying sources of energy loss. By comparing two designs, we demonstrate that a cavity with a more intricate geometry enables both larger envelope areas and tighter mode confinement, allowing for efficient coupling to a high-impedance bath while maintaining spectral properties. This terahertz-feasible analysis provides a promising approach for evaluating and improving quantum devices. Moreover, we successfully integrate Josephson junctions with long-wavelength plasmons in micromechanical systems, demonstrating a new type of mechanical resonator with a wide frequency range. This research is a significant step towards developing functional quantum processors. A companion Git repository contains the design files for resonators discussed in this study. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also review the major factors that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including magmatic, geological, and climatic processes, as well as their long-term geological controls. These processes include planetary differentiation, mantle convection, surface tectonics, and atmospheric evolution, with associated timescales of 4.5 billion years. We then discuss the observed state of the atmosphere, presenting a comprehensive overview of its current composition, with a focus on the elemental and isotopic abundances of atmospheric gases. We also analyze the atmospheric escape mechanisms that have acted over time, with a focus on how they have influenced the planet's inventory of volatiles. We examine the observed state of the atmosphere in relation to the planet's interior, with a focus on the interactions between the core, mantle, and crust, and their effects on the atmosphere's evolution. We also discuss the major feedback mechanisms that have shaped the atmosphere's evolution, with a focus on how they have influenced the planet's thermal state, surface geology, and chemistry, as well as the atmospheric circulation and volatile inventory. We then outline the key uncertainties in our understanding of the atmosphere's evolution and present a comprehensive model of the long-term development of Venus's atmosphere, with a focus on the interactions between the interior and exterior processes that have shaped its composition over time. We also discuss the implications of this model for our understanding of the planet's evolution and provide a set of testable predictions that can guide ongoing and future research, with a focus on how to better constrain the long-term development of Venus's atmosphere. We conclude by examining the broader implications of this work for exoplanetary research and the search for Earth-like planets, with a focus on how it can inform the prioritization of targets for biosignature analysis. We also discuss the role of high-resolution spectroscopy in searching for biomarkers in the atmospheres of terrestrial planets similar to Earth, with a focus on how it can be used to detect signs of life on planets with surface temperatures similar to those of Venus. This research develops a Bayesian method for assessing nonlinear Hawkes processes, which are marked point processes characterized by feedback loops. These processes are often used to model systems with reciprocal connections, such as information flows on social media or brain activity in the human brain. We created a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm to estimate the nonlinearity of these processes and identified suitable Bayesian credible regions for the model's parameters. Additionally, we designed a statistical approach to compare the nonlinearity of two populations or time periods. This involves calculating the difference in the parameter space, which can be interpreted as a measure of the difference in the populations' nonlinearity. We demonstrated and validated our method using both artificial and real-world data, including Twitter data on stock market announcements and electroencephalogram recordings from humans listening to those announcements. These applications enable a deeper understanding of how information spreads and patterns form through reciprocal connections. Sincerely, Armand A. Berthet and Joseph T. Sakella. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics, such as damage and limited reflectivity, hinder further development. In this research, we investigate alternatives to traditional waveplates that can both shift the laser polarization and enhance its intensity in magnetized plasmas. A specific scenario is examined where a $4$-gram gas plasma is positioned at a $10$-cm distance from the end of a fiber, allowing it to function as a $\pi/2$-waveplate and increasing the laser's intensity by more than $20$ while shifting its polarization. This achievement is attributed to the unique interaction between the $10.53$-micron wavelength of the $CO_2$ laser used to create the plasma and the $1$-cm magnetic field length, which together produce a $3.4$-microradian specific interaction that results in a $0.25$-radian overall phase shift and a $\pi/2$-polarization transformation. This breakthrough suggests that carefully designed magnetized plasmas can safely handle multi-petawatt laser pulses near their focus, enabling the development of powerful plasma waveplates that can both alter and intensify high-powered laser beams. This advancement has implications for multiple applications, including particle acceleration, inertial fusion, and astrophysical plasma studies. We provide a proof that this equation holds when the triangulation is topologically consistent, meaning it forms a simplicial complex. This form of the equation then serves as a basis for demonstrating that the Pontrjagin class of an abstract simplicial complex is invariant under topological restructions of the simplicial complex. This invariance in turn enables the definition of the Pontrjagin class of an abstract simplicial complex as the intrinsic, geometric property it is recognized to be. This proof builds on and updates our previous work from 2000, with additional generalization to the oriented case. It also introduces a more fundamental principle of geometric invariance that underlies the relationship between the Pontrjagin class and the boundary of a manifold. This principle can be interpreted as a differential equation in the combinatorial sense, and its application to the oriented case yields a new and distinct formula for the total Pontrjagin class. This formula can also be obtained through the use of the Pontrjagin-Andersson Schubert calculus. This note concludes with the suggestion that a similar principle of invariance may be found as a basis for the definition of the Rochlitz-Selberg formula for the Euler characteristic of a simplicial complex. This note is composed of an introductory section, followed by three mathematical sections. The first mathematical section proves the validity of the Gelfand-MacPherson equation for triangulations of a closed, connected, orientable surface of any genus. This is accomplished through the use of graphical methods and the analysis of loop configurations. The second mathematical section demonstrates that the Pontrjagin class of a simplicial complex is invariant under the process of simplifying a surface through the removal of horns from a simplicial complex. This invariance serves as a basis for the definition of the Pontrjagin class of an abstract simplicial complex. The third mathematical section generalizes this principle of invariance to the oriented case and presents a distinct formula for the total Pontrjagin class, and also discusses its relationship with the Pontrjagin-Andersson Schubert calculus. We have developed a novel numerical approach for obtaining the equilibrium configurations of rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, utilizing a pseudo-Eulerian formulation, incorporates a simple and effective pre-processing step to determine the distribution of specific angular momentum within the star, thus bypassing the need for direct integration of the rotation equations in the calculation of equilibrium configurations. By combining this with an efficient time-stepping scheme for the Eulerian formulation of the Einstein equations, our method allows for the direct calculation of the evolution of rotating stars over time. In our initial application, we determine and compare the equilibrium configurations of rotating stars under both general relativity and Newtonian gravity, using models of uniform and gradient-specific angular momentum. These comparisons serve as a foundation for extending our research to the dynamic evolution of rotating stars, such as rotating white dwarfs and neutron stars that have undergone mass transfer in their evolution. This new approach provides a valuable tool for investigating these and other astrophysical phenomena. This work was featured in a previous arXiv post, arXXiv:2105.12337. However, as the number of detected mergers continues to rise, a manually pre-selected event list may become impractical. Therefore, developing an all-sky surveillance system with the capability to identify and categorize all detected signals is crucial. Presently, matching signal models to observed data is computationally intensive and typically filtered through matched filters prior to further analysis. To understand the impact of the pandemic on urban diversity, we analyzed changes in users' activity patterns on a popular mobile location-sharing platform, particularly focusing on income-related variations. Our data span the initial pandemic period from February to July 2020 and cover 16 major global cities. We identified reduced social connectivity and altered mobility patterns during the pandemic, with varying intensity across different cities. Notably, we observed decreased diversity in users' encounters in 9 out of the 16 studied cities. When considering factors that could influence these changes, we found that the shift towards less diverse encounters was more pronounced in cities with higher pre-pandemic income diversification. This trend suggests that the pandemic may have exacerbated income-related differences in urban social encounters, contrary to expectations that it would decrease diversity altogether. We also identified increased repetition in users' encounters in 12 cities, which could be a result of users with similar mobility patterns congregating more closely during the pandemic. When examining the factors contributing to increased repetition, we found that it was more significant in cities with greater geographical diversity, as well as those with higher pre-pandemic income levels. These findings and the use of mobile data to analyze income-related variations in urban encounters provide new insights for researchers and policymakers working to mitigate the pandemic's lasting social effects. A significant portion of massive star-forming cores harbor multiple protostars rather than a single one. This phenomenon can either lead to the formation of binary or multiple stars, potentially influencing the evolution and ultimate fate of the formed star. Until recently, it was primarily optical and infrared observations that discovered multiple-protein systems in massive cores, with millimeter observations revealing only rare examples. This study examines the submillimeter observation data of massive star-forming cores and investigates the prevalence of multiple-protein systems, focusing on whether they often have closely spaced separations that could result from core fragmentation, or more distant protostars that may have formed through gravitational collapse of a dense ridge. It also analyzes the possible outcomes of such systems, including the potential for one star to consume the other, and assesses the impact on the surrounding environment, including nearby outflows, ridges, and newly formed stellar clusters. The study presents a simple model of dust continuum emission that can be used to recover reliable main sequence stars and estimates the frequencies of binary and multiple star formations in massive cores, and the probable masses of these stars based on observations and modeling of 106 protostar-containing cores across the Milky Way and nearby galaxies. This research investigates how a uniform current affects water waves in a Hamiltonian manner by developing a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation with constant circulation, thereby providing a more comprehensive model that incorporates rotation. Offering a more accurate representation, this new equation surpasses the existing Dysthe model, especially in regards to energy-based metrics. Both the new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation and the existing Dysthe model are proven to be good approximations for weakly nonlinear, long-wavelength waves in a Hamiltonian context, and their differences are analyzed to determine when each model is most applicable. Ultimately, our research reveals that both models can be valid in the same parameter range, thereby justifying their collective use in scientific studies. As a practical demonstration, we apply these models to predict wave transformations during two-dimensional experiments featuring a varying slope of incline, and show that both models accurately describe these transformations across a broad spectrum of parameters. As a notable addition, our work incorporates a new approach for dealing with the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation, specifically the Hamiltonian Dysthe formulation of constant circulation, which can be obtained through a direct application of the Hamiltonian Dysthe transformation to the Hamiltonian form of the problem. This new formulation becomes a non-local Hamiltonian system when both circulation and the current speed are constant, which provides a new perspective on this problem. As a broader contribution, our research develops several tools for analyzing the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation of constant circulation, which can be used to study more complex, variable circulation cases. These tools involve a new energy-based $H^1$ well-posedness result, a new global-in-time result for an initial value problem, and a new proof of the convergence of the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation to the Hamiltonian KdV equation. These results can all be applied to the new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation of constant circulation, as well as to a more general, variable circulation case. Which in turn allows us to generate a well-posedness result for a wide class of Hamiltonian Dysthe equations, along with global-in-time results and convergence results for a wide range of nonlinear wave problems. Which further indicates that our approach can be used as a framework for studying a broad category of Hamiltonian Dysthe equations, and provides a set of tools that can be used to analyze these equations in a Hamiltonian context. This paper introduces a concept of differential forms with values in a module that varies over a given space, building on the foundation of G-Differential forms. A significant outcome of this approach is the derived Stokes formula for forms with values in a module that changes with position. To derive the formula's proof, we establish an appropriate integration module that remains unchanged under the differential shape structure. This integration module serves as the target for the Stokes operator in this context. If the underlying space is compact, we can also define and compute integrals of forms with values in a module that changes with position. In addition, we introduce the concept of cohomologous modules, and provide an expression for the output of the Stokes operator in terms of these modules. If the space is path-connected, we can further establish that two modules are isomorphic, which in turn allows us to define and compute the integral of forms with values in a module that changes with position, using an approach based on differential characters. Similar outcomes can be obtained using an alternative method building on the Cech procedure. A key aspect of this work is that it minimally assumes the continuity of the module-defining map, and does not require it to be smooth. As such, this paper also discusses the corresponding results for forms with values in a module that changes with position, in the special case of a smooth context. In this smooth case, we can also establish that the output of the Stokes operator at any given point is equal to the result of integrating forms with values in a module that changes with position, over that point. As a specific example, we consider a module that changes with position and has a specific variation, and show that its integral can be computed using the derived Stokes formula. Furthermore, we establish that this module defining the differential forms is isomorphic to the module that includes differential forms multiplied by the module that changes with position, and provide an expression for the output of the Stokes operator in terms of these modules. In addition, we discuss its applications in the context of a second-order differential operator. A key factor in navigating safely on the surface or underwater is effective environment perception. While visual and sonar sensors are widely used for this purpose, they often require extensive computational resources to combine their information, especially in real-time scenarios. This issue is particularly problematic for embedded systems on drones, robots, and other mobile devices with limited processing power. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach that integrates sonar sensors with a biologically-inspired navigation system, enabling a freely-wandering and target-seeking behavior in real-time on various platforms. We demonstrate this approach on an ESP32-CAM drone and an Intel Galileo board, showing that it can combine sonar and visual data to navigate through complex obstacles in both indoor and outdoor environments. This integration on the ESP32-CAM results in a significant decrease in frame rates, from 15 to 8 FPS, while on the Intel Galileo board it drops from 25 to 20 FPS. This research provides a basic framework for navigating using multiple sensors in various applications, including underwater environments. Although it was tested underwater, we emphasize that the sonar used here is a $10 CMOS sonar that is not truly "underwater" as it is designed to function in both air and water but may not work in deep water scenarios with significant water pressure." This statement holds true based on general sensor knowledge and has not been verified through actual underwater testing of this specific device. This research can be extended to various frequencies of sonar devices, different navigation modes, and a range of environments. All the code used in this project is available open-source on GitHub at https://github.com/AbdullahAlDurra/Real-Time-Sonar-Integration.

Contrary to prior research, $\textsc{twist}\textsc{row}$ is unaffected by rotational ambiguities that plague other methods through applying a rotational invariance technique. Moreover, $\textsc{twist}\textsc{row}$ overcomes issues with nonconvex relaxations by employing an iterative algorithm that leverages both convex and nonconvex projections. Experimentation with $\textsc{twist}\textsc{row}$ on actual data sets reveals its superiority in terms of both solution quality and computational efficiency compared to state-of-the-art algorithms. The results indicate a notable improvement of about two orders of magnitude in terms of the number of iterations required for convergence, which is a critical advancement given the typically large data sets this algorithm is designed to handle. Traditionally, annotated data have served as training and evaluation bases for natural language processing tasks. Yet, contemporary models have shown potential in using unannotated data as references for annotation. In this work, we leverage pre-trained language models to guide the semantic annotation of emotion-related questions. A style of intervention is employed to direct the model in identifying areas needing annotated labels. From a practical standpoint, we derive a straightforward method for correcting annotations based on model-predicted label probabilities. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we established a dataset containing annotated and corresponding correction suggestions for emotion-related questions. Our results show that, using both a simple baseline and a more complex evaluation involving the suggested annotations, the potential for BERT-enabled correction guidance is substantial. Furthermore, we reveal the scope for integrating additional features such as multiple neural network models and handcrafted criteria: incorporating these features leads to a notable improvement in annotation correction. Finally, we highlight potential applications in using BERT to facilitate the annotation of lesser-studied emotion-related question types. The underlying code and a newly established dataset are available for public use.

As object-based programming on GPUs has a growing need to counterbalance raw computation speed with efficient memory management, parallel memory allocation has become a critical performance bottleneck. To address this limitation, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed specifically for object-based GPU applications. Featuring a unique, three-tiered allocation system, DynaSOAr prioritizes high-speed memory access by concentrating small objects in a compact, cache-friendly block. This approach allows for significantly faster and more energy-efficient memory operations, with our tests demonstrating a 5-fold and a 4-fold improvement in allocation and deallocation time respectively. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's efficient fragmentation-reducing technique and tailored thread-safe synchronization component for global memory blocks enhance overall performance and scalability. By optimizing both internal memory access and external communication, DynaSOAr's allocation and deallocation functions outperform current state-of-the-art solutions by approximately 2.5 times when using a large memory block, and our tests show that DynaSOAr is compatible with major overlying object-based languages for GPU programming. With an average allocation time of 43.9 cycles, DynaSOAr sets a new benchmark for memory allocation on GPUs, paving the way for the development of high-performance, object-based GPU applications with efficient memory management. To facilitate widespread adoption, DynaSOAr's source code has been made publicly available as an open-source project.

By calculating the band structures and analyzing the charge distribution, we evaluated the effect of these impurities on the band gap of TiO2.  Both carbon and nitrogen can form different types of bonds with the Ti or O atoms in the TiO2 lattice, resulting in multiple possible doped structures.  However, only one-dimensional chains and a magnetic "ladder" structure were observed when using nitrogen as a dopant.  These results suggest that N-doped TiO2 may exhibit both metallic and magnetic properties, dependent on the dopant concentration, which could provide explanations for experimental anomalies and offer new applications for this material.  Notably, the "ladder" structure may also be relevant to other transition metal doped TiO2 lattices. This proposal leverages the Large Hadron Collider's capability to produce protons at an extreme intensity, taking advantage of a long-standing observation that highly energetic gluons play a significant role in particle collisions. We suggest taking the forward direction of the collider, where the intense gluons in two protons could collide and combine to create a pair of top-quarks and quarks or antiquarks via an "effective" elastic interaction. We estimate that approximately 50 top-quark pairs per year could be detected at the Large Hadron Collider's 13-TeV energy level, primarily consisting of top-quark pairs with significant momentum in the forward direction. A dedicated trigger algorithm is proposed to identify these events efficiently. We also outline potential paths for analyzing these events, including a simple approach using variables that characterize the rapidities of the detected particles, a more in-depth study utilizing jet substructure in the forward region, and an exploration of specialized techniques that could be developed in the future. These predictions and analysis suggestions emphasize the Large Hadron Collider's versatility in discovering new physics through elastic processes with forward jet production. Given the large amount of data that the Large Hadron Collider will continue to generate, detecting elastic top-quark pairs at higher energy levels, such as 13.6 TeV, could significantly increase the recorded event count to thousands per year, offering ample opportunities for extracting precise information about the energy distribution of the gluons in protons. This could be particularly valuable in establishing a reliable approach to studying the quark gluon plasma in deep collision experiments at the Large Hadron Collider and future high-energy particle colliders. In 1964, Erdos and Galai posed a problem that led to further research and a more general question from Ramsey theory. This note addresses one aspect of that general question by establishing an infinite graph Ramsey property, which we've termed upper richness. It surpasses the equivalent properties previously established by Sauer and Miller. Upper richness can be found in infinite subgraphs of infinite countable graphs that contain every finite subgraph at least once. Notably, there are infinite upper rich subgraphs within the randomly constructed graph from Erdos and Spinka. Additionally, we examine the relationship between upper richness and another property called high complexity. This leads to a distinction from the results found by Duran and Todorcev. Our analysis also considers the upper richness of edge-colouring preserving subgraphs. Notably, these subgraphs have a different and more intricate Ramsey property. This property demands that every finite edge set is contained within a finite factor of the same cardinality. This edge property is not equivalent to the equivalent properties previously established by us, and it enables us to conclude that there is an edge-coloured upper rich subgraph that is not isomorphic to any edge-coloured subgraph of the randomly constructed graph from Erdos and Spinka.
